subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES. 1973-74 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD

speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1974, was presented by Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board) and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES. 1973-74 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to table the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1974.
The main estimates for 1973-74 tabled today propose budgetary expenditures of $18,393 million and non-budgetary expenditures-that is, loans, investments and advances-of $893 million.
In the Speech from the Throne made in early January, this government reaffirmed its long standing commitment to the all-important goals of national unity and equality of opportunity for all Canadians. It spoke as well of the measures it would lay before parliament in the fields of
economic policy and social policy toward the achievement of these goals.
You will find, Mr. Speaker, that in furtherance of social policy objectives, these estimates contemplate higher expenditures for such programs as public housing and land development; assistance to native peoples; unconditional transfer payments to the provinces that permit greater equality in provincial services; bilingualism; and payments to provinces to assist them in financing hospital, medical and welfare services.
Higher expenditures are also proposed to strengthen the economy, notably through assistance to the technological development of our industry, to the orderly development of northern transportation and to other fields of transportation and communications throughout the country.
In certain other cases, where decisions were taken too late to be reflected in the main estimates, funding proposals will be submitted to parliament during the course of the fiscal year.
The government also spoke of a high degree of professionalism as being the primary and most essential objective of the armed forces. Hon. members will note a significant addition to the defence estimates with the lifting of the ceiling placed on the expenditures of the Department of National Defence in 1970-71.
The total increase of $2,274 million in estimates for budgetary expenditures for the coming year over forecast expenditures for the current year is unusually large. About 40 per cent of this increase arises because last year, the transitional year between the old and the new unemployment insurance plan, there were no budgetary expenditures for the commission, while the estimates for the coming year contain $890 million as the payment, after the fact, of the government's contribution to unemployment benefit payments in calendar year 1972. This does not call for any actual cash flow since the contribution is more than covered by the money already advanced to the commission over the past months.
Two years ago this government began to issue a companion booklet to the estimates called "How Your Tax Dollar is Spent". It is designed to better inform the public on the use made by the government of the revenues collected.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES. 1973-74 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we face today a novel situation in that on the day after the presentation of the budget, in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) outlined the methods whereby he proposes to raise money to cover the government's spending program, we are presented with the blue book of main estimates. It would have been far better, I suggest, if this had been done earlier provided the government was ready to do so. I suggest that the government was ready because the tabling of the estimates has been an on and off matter for the past two or three weeks. Actually, if one recalls events of about two weeks ago, it will be remembered that the estimates were to be tabled on Wednesday, and then on Thursday. The matter has been deferred from day to day. We should like to know the rationale of the government in choosing to bring in the main spending estimates on the day after the presentation of the budget.
The estimates disclose some interesting things. Having had the blue book delivered to me about 90 seconds ago, I do not think hon. members would expect me to be able to make a detailed analysis. The minister made a short statement indicating that the total estimates exceed those of last year by $2,200 million. That, in itself, is quite a revelation.
I am also conscious of the fact that he disclosed that the estimates this year will cover the deficiency in the unemployment insurance program last year, something which was vehemently denied. The government attempted to cover this up in many ways during the consideration of supplementary estimates. The minister can shake his head, but I suggest that many attempts were made to cover up the precise amount of the deficiency in the program. The minister and his colleagues tried to play a shell game with us in this regard.
We shall be examining the estimates in detail. They will now be sent to the various committees for study. I expect that some of the glow that seems to have arisen from last night's budgetary performance will undoubtedly be dissipated when we look at the blue book and see how the government proposes to spend those billions of dollars which are coming out of the pockets of Canadian taxpayers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the last sentence spoken by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) was the only relevant one to make at this time in that tomorrow we will begin the budget debate in which we will discuss the general policies of the government. These estimates will go to the various committees of the House to be studied. I hope that some weeks from now we will know more about the details of the estimates than we know now. I see no reason for taking any more of the time of the House.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES. 1973-74 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some very brief comments to make in this connection.
I thank the President of the Treasury Board for having given us a copy of his statement. We will have the oppor-

tunity to discuss further during the debate on the budget beginning tomorrow.
I note that last sentence of the minister's statement which reads as follows:
The special theme of this year's issue is the programs which assist the consumers as he buys goods and services in the market place.
This idea was taken up yesterday in the budget speech and it could be noted that the government was increasingly dwelling on the consideration of the Canadian consumers' problems concerning national production. The government is showing a good intention as it was seen in some measures announced yesterday-not all of them.
Mr. Speaker, this is not new for the Social Crediters for, since we have been elected to the House, we have been urging the government to give all its attention to the consumer problem in Canada. It is nice to produce for billions of dollars but if that production does not reach its final end which is consumption then we will experience problems as those we have been and are still experiencing: inflation, unemployment and poverty in a very wealthy country.
I take the opportunity offered by the tabling of the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1973 to draw the attention of the House on table No 4 which appears on page 32 of Chapter 1, under the title: Percentage Distribution by Function 1973-74.
Despite the good intentions of the government, the fact remains that it will spend 14 per cent of its budget on the public debt. That represents $2,581 million in taxpayers' money which will be paid out to strangers, big companies, in interest only, without reducing the principal. Does that reflect an improvement or a worsening of the situation?
We already see in that column that the interest on the public debt will go up by $405,600,000 this year.
Mr. Speaker, this means that the measures announced yesterday by the expansionary budget of the minority government-which has no alternative but to listen to the demands of the opposition parties, including the Social Credit party-confirm the fact that the government does not really have any financial solution to propose. While encouraging economic expansion, it should reduce the public debt and enable Canadians to become in fact the masters of their own economy.
Therefore I deeply regret this method of financing Canada's debt and I say to the hon. minister that it is time more than ever for his government, instead of laughing at the Social credit suggestions, to consider our proposal or any alternative serious proposal which could make possible the financing of this item.
I conclusion, I would say that if we assign 14 per cent of the budget for servicing the public debt, only 13.2 per cent is allowed for economic expansion in Canada and this proves that it is more important for the present government to help financiers than to develop Canada.
February 20, 1973

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. When the committee rose at five o'clock yesterday, votes 5, 35, 40a, 45a in the schedule relating to the Department of National Health and Welfare were being considered, and the hon. member for Lotbiniere had the floor.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday I asked for the opportunity to say a few words on items 35a and 40a. Shortly after the adjournment of the debate yesterday, the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) announced in the budget speech something which is related to these
February 20, 1973

items, namely the old age security pension and basic rates which differ from those we discussed yesterday afternoon.
Mr. Chairman, I would have spoken any way about the age of eligibility for the old age security pension. When we read the report of the special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Poverty in Canada as regards the dependency of many Canadians, we note that they recommend that a guaranteed income be given to a maximum number of Canadians who find themselves in a state of dependency.
The reading of the annual reviews of the Economic Council of Canada, allows one to draw similar conclusions; when one reads the Speech from the Throne made at the very beginning of this session, one will note once again the good intentions of this government which is talking about implementing a guaranteed income scheme.
In view of the budget presented last night-which could be predicted yesterday afternoon-the government agreed, after numerous representations and pressures from the Social Credit party of Canada, to increase old age security pensions. We were asking $350 a month and the government agreed to approximate that amount with $325 a month. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this is a gain for our party which proves that our requests are not always ridiculous since the government is forced to agree to our proposals one day or another.
We have been asking for a long time that the government consider in the context of a guaranteed income scheme, the possibility of lowering to 60 the retirement age in Canada so that if one person receives old age security at 60, his spouse, whatever his age may be, could be entitled to the old age pension. I take the opportunity offered to draw the government's attention on that important matter.
Since the government is in a minority position, since it cannot be as arrogant as it has been since 1968 and since it must take account of our claims, it agrees partly to what we have been asking. However, that does not imply that it will get our whole support.
In view of the problems facing our fellow citizens, it is essential that the government and the minister undertake, as for the examination of votes 35a and 40a, to give details more rapidly than it had forecasted, since the budget was presented last night, on the possibility of first lowering eligibility for old age security pension to 60 and, second granting the old age pension automatically to both spouses when one has reached the pensionable age.
Then, Mr. Chairman, if the government agrees to work for the liberalization of the human being in order to give him an economic security in this country, it will not only show its good will but also that it understands many citizens who live in poverty and dependency.
Mr. Chairman, the old age security pension as it now exists in Canada often gives rise to dissatisfaction. The basic pension of $82.88, which is now increased to $100, is a statutory pension, according to the statement of the hon. minister.
If someone cannot make both ends meet with this basic pension, then the whole mechanism of the oppressive bureaucracy gets started to have forms signed, to check
Supply
the claimants' ressources and if they are more or less dependent they will be entitled to the garanteed income supplement.
Mr. Chairman, this is just administrative make work which imply very substantial expenditures for the administration of the old age security pension. We in the Social Credit Party feel that it would be a lot easier to grant an equal pension to all Canadians who are 60 years old, which would make the administration of this program easier and would permit an increase in the old age pensions, thanks to the money that would be saved.
Mr. Chairman, during the question period today and the debate yesterday the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) committed himself to announce his plans to the House as to the age of eligibility. He said that first he had to meet with the representatives of provincial governments.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare that this House has a right to know what his intentions are in this regard even before he discusses the matter with the provinces. The minister should realize that provinces have some jurisdiction in that field-we acknowledge it-and that parliament which represents the people of Canada should have its say in the setting of the guidelines of the social security policy in Canada, regardless of what the provinces think.
That does not mean, Mr. Chairman, that we should not object to the policy proposed by the provinces. Of course, we must look for efficient and continuous consultation with other levels of government. But the minister should realize the importance of consulting his colleagues to set up the policy and I am sure that he will get excellent advice from all members of this House, particularly from the Social Credit party of Canada.
I remember the time when the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Caouette) was proposing to set old age pensions at $75 a month when they were much lower than that. Both Liberals and Progressive Conservatives-it's all the same-were saying: Caouette is sick. Caouette is mad. It doesn't make sense. Now the first time one of these parties managed to remain in power, it increased the old age pension by $25 over and above what the Social Credit leader was asking for, which makes the national leader say, and justly so, that the old parties are late and at least 25 times sicker than he was then.
Since I came to the House I noticed that some of our colleagues, smarter than others, have a tendency to ridicule certain points of the Social Credit doctrine as well as some of our proposals. I pointed out on motions, in reply to a statement from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) an item of the estimates introduced yesterday which shows that 14.2 per cent of the total budget will be appropriated for servicing the public debt which for this present year amounts to $2.5 billion. Yet no hon. member of the other parties has brought up this matter. Maybe it has no importance, but I will point out to my hon. colleagues that this item alone entails an increase of $450 million in this year's budget.
When you consider that over the same period of time only 13.2 per cent of the budget is devoted to economic

February 20, 1973
Supply
expansion, you realize that the Creditistes are not as crazy as they are said to be. They are probably right when they urge the House to vote new credits to finance Canada's normal development, including social security.
When the government announces tax cuts so as to raise the old age security pensions, it is at the same time forced to increase the public debt and to present a deficit budget. Everyone indeed knows that this year's deficit will amount to $2 billion.
I asked the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) what measures he intends to take to finance this deficit-which was an important question. The hon. minister-everyone heard his reply-does not know. He said that he cannot do otherwise than use the two normal solutions which have been used for 100 years, namely government bonds and taxes.
In both cases, these solutions would reduce the taxpayers' purchasing power and boost our national debt. So, the more it goes, the more it is the same, and when the government grants tax cuts to save its skin, it has to increase the national, municipal and provincial debts. In brief, it has no long or short term solution to pay those debts.
The House is now requested to carry credits 35a and 40a totalling $5,385,000 for only a small portion of social security. But considering the cost of operating that program because there are so many forms to fill, the length of the negotiations and studies which never lead to concrete solutions, the increasingly dependent condition of most of our citizens in this country, which is a rich country, I think that if we claim some degree of intellectual honesty, we will have, in spite of ourselves, one of these days to consider this other Social Credit proposal which is to ensure each Canadian citizen of a guaranteed annual income through the issue of new credits from the Bank of Canada, thus avoiding getting Canadians into debt while granting them their share of the national product.
The minister gave an idea of his great plans in the Speech from the Throne, but after reading last night's budget speech we realize that the Minister of Finance did not dare to consult his colleague in National Health and Welfare Department since there is not a word about this in his budget.
Mr. Chairman, the government is not able to bring about the guaranteed annual income for all Canadian citizens. This government, as well as those who would want to replace it, the Progressive Conservatives, have no way of ensuring income security for Canadian citizens. And these same Progressive Conservatives want to govern the country.
Mr. Chairman, once more I ask the government what is the meaning of the credits the House is asked to vote since they only increase taxes and only minimal amounts are left.
Mr. Chairman, we should stop asking ourselves whether we have the means. It is obvious that we would have the means if we stopped getting Canadians into debt through abnormal financing procedures, namely taxes and Canada savings bonds.
The government has a financial tool on hand, that is the Bank of Canada. It should be used not just any old way

but in accordance with a regular procedure and within the framework of a balanced budget in order to give a guaranteed income to all Canadians, specially to the citizens as soon as they reach 60. Thanks to this measure, our older citizens will no longer fell left out.
In conclusion, I would like to relate to the minister a very typical example in order to prove the importance of this proposal. I know for a fact that there are in my riding many cases where the 65 year-old worker is no longer able to work for reasons of poor health. So he retires and gets a piddling pension from the government. The pension will be better now, but is it truly enough?
If a spouse who retires and stays put at home wants to receive the guaranteed income supplement, he will go and fill out a form. Then someone will check his bank account, find out whether or not he reports the interest on his savings and check as well whether he gets additional income from rents, etc. Because of what he receives and the fact that his wife is not yet 65 years old, his pension, his sole income, will not be enough. What happens in such cases? The wife, who is probably 62 or 63, and also probably ill and less capable of working than at 23, will go out and wash floors, do dishes in restaurants or hotels to earn $15, $25, $30 or $40 more to make ends meet.
Mr. Chairman, in such cases, the government is primarily responsible for the state of slavery, dependence in which Canadians find themselves who are no longer capable, in certain circumstances of fighting for themselves, because of the inflated economic situation we are in.
Mr. Chairman, that is why I request, with my colleagues of the Social Credit party, that the old age security pension be given automatically to married couples as soon as one of the spouses reaches age 60, this to enable them to live together, to rest and take advantage of their retirement without any financial worries.
To my mind, that is the primary role of the government and the minister would be well advised to tell us what is his position is in this regard, before we pass the votes before the House.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take up the time of the committee for very long. I wish to refer specifically to certain serious administrative problems which the Minister of National Health and Welfare faces in this department. I am raising this subject today because there is often difficulty in bringing up urgent matters of this kind during the question period.
I am not attributing blame specifically to the minister. After all, he is a new minister. I would blame the former minister, if anyone. But this is a matter which the hon. gentleman might well look into. I am sure he has received complaints at one time or another from almost every member in the House. Anyhow, he certainly will be receiving such complaints. This leads me to the question of disabled allowances-disability pensions under the Canada Pension Plan. In this regard, a letter sent out under the minister's signature describes what constitutes disability under the terms of the plan. He said:
February 20, 1973

The legislation provides that a person must be suffering from both a severe and prolonged mental or physical disability.
That is simple enough.
Under the legislation, "severe" means that a person must be incapable regularly of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation by reason of mental or physical disability. "Prolonged" means that incapacity to work at any substantially gainful occupation will be present for a long continued and indefinite period of time.
This all seems fairly simple. One would not suppose it would lead to any great difficulty in interpretation. But there have been many complaints about the way in which this part of the plan is administered, and it would seem to me that in the case of nearly all the complaints brought to my attention the conditions stated have been fulfilled.
Apparently, there is some medical board which carries out certain duties under the minister's instructions. We are told, in reply to questions recently placed on the order paper, that there are 13 doctors who possess certain qualifications for making decisions in these cases. It was also interesting to learn, in an answer on February 14 last to a question by my hon. friend from Simcoe North, that after an application has been received, "along with medical and other reports"-I don't know what that means; perhaps the minister could tell us-the applicant is asked to undergo an examination if it is felt that further medical information is required. Mr. Chairman, I should like to know, very specifically, just what constitutes these mysterious "other reports". Who sends them in? Where do they come from? What is the nature of these "other reports"? It is necessary, I suppose, for someone in the minister's department to decide that the terms of the act are being carried out, but the information required by the board is purely medical information, supplied, usually, by a family doctor or a clinic. But the board chooses to disregard it in many cases, apparently, and this leads to serious questions being raised in parliament.
I ask the minister to check very carefully into this board of so-called medical advisers. I do not want to go into detail, and name names, because that is not the practice in this House. But I think the minister might look over the qualifications-I do not mean the paper qualifications but the actual qualifications-of some of the medical advisers who are supposed to be doctors. I am informed by my hon. friend from Cape Breton-East Richmond that on one occasion one of these advisers appearing at a hearing seemed to be, at least, somewhat politically inclined, if not very knowledgeable. He said: "There are three things which are certain in this world. One is death, one is taxes and the other is the re-election of a Liberal government". It seems very strange indeed that medical evidence of this nature should be given.
Right in front of me I have documents relating to three cases which I have brought to the minister's attention. I do not suppose he ever actually saw them. Probably he did not. I have been here long enough to know how these things go. In one case, an applicant who was turned down a couple of times by this medical board, had lost a leg. The other was to be removed. I do not know whether or not he will be considered disabled. Apparently not by the board. But he would appear rather disabled to me. I do not see how he can do very much work in the future. His disability will certainly be prolonged, I would think. In another case, the man concerned is suffering from
Supply
emphysema. I think it is common knowledge among members of this House that those who suffer from emphysema are not allowed to do heavy work, if any work at all. In fact, they are lucky if they can walk across the room or breathe. Another case I have before me at the moment concerns a lady in her late fifties who has suffered repeated cardiac arrests. On one occasion, the only reason she didn't die, according to a report from her family doctor, was that she happened to be in an intensive care unit. The prognosis in this case is by no means good, yet she is not considered to be disabled.
This kind of thing must be brought to the minister's attention. If he is a good minister, as I think he probably is, he should check very carefully into the kind of judgment which is passed out by this so-called board of medical advisers and find out the nature of these other mysterious reports which they are supposed to read. Will he give some personal attention to this matter, or appoint somebody to look into it, because a great many people across Canada are affected? I am sure every member of this House has received correspondence from his constituency on the subject. It is purely an administrative problem and I believe the minister should exercise, as soon as he can, his administrative authority in this regard.

I should like to say a few words on the subject which my hon. friend from Oxford has brought to the attention of the committee. What we are dealing with, now, is the examination which takes place under the Canada Pension Plan in connection with applications for disability pensions. It appears a person has to be dying before he can qualify. From an examination of the list showing the number of applicants rejected it would appear that the conditions are getting tougher every year, despite the fact that increasing numbers of people are unemployed. In 1970, 78 per cent of the applicants, or 3,087, were determined as being disabled and 16.9 per cent were determined as being not disabled. In 1971, there were 10,019 applicants, 78.5 per cent of whom were listed as disabled and 17.7 per cent of whom were refused. In 1972, we find the ratio of those refused pensions had risen. Only 74 per cent passed and 22 per cent were refused. These figures reflect an increasingly tougher position in the granting of disability pensions. Looking at the situation from the point of view of the economy, I would think this trend should be reversed at a time when more than 600,000 people in Canada are unemployed. Leniency should be shown when a man is sick and becomes unemployable.
I have just one case history here. The person concerned underwent five operations, I think, two for cancer; his gall bladder and stomach have been removed; he was in hospital three times during the first four or five months of last year. Yet his application for a disability pension has been rejected. There is something very peculiar about the whole business. I am astounded to learn that the word of a general practitioner is not accepted, or even of the internist who examines an applicant locally. The board simply wishes to hear what treatment has been prescribed, and then makes up its own mind. This goes against everything we know of medicine, because the doctor who clinically examines a patient, knowing the history of the case, is in a better position to know the facts than anyone who sits

February 20, 1973
Supply
down at a desk and makes a ruling on the basis of a report.
We learn that the applicants' own physicians are not asked to determine whether a person is disabled under the terms of the Canada Pension Plan legislation, on the ground that a decision is more than purely medical in nature. So the decision is more than purely medical in nature! As the hon. member for Oxford asked, what else is it? What is being hidden? The standard reply of the department goes on to say that the decision must be made, as required by the legislation, by the Canada Pension Plan administration. As the hon. member for Oxford also pointed out, here is the administration itself deciding whether or not a man is disabled.
The reply continues, and I quote:
The applicant's physician is simply asked for objective findings of any functional limitations.
It is something like playing checkers at a distance and you phone in your moves.
This procedure, including the medical report form answered by physicians, was approved by a committee of experts on disability assessment-
I should certainly like to meet these experts, as I am sure would other hon. members of the House who have had some difficulty with the CPP administration. The reply continues:
The statistics of the nature requested are not kept since the applicant's physician is only forwarding a medical report; that is, the physicians are requested to report their objective findings rather than to provide their opinion as to whether the applicant meets the requirements of the Canada Pension Plan legislation.
Can you beat that, Mr. Chairman? I am sure that the minister feels he has a lot of cleaning up to do in his department. The reply continues:
After the application is received along with the medical and other reports, if it is felt that more medical information is required the applicant is asked to undergo an examination by a medical specialist (consultant) at Canada Pension Plan expense. With this information, a large number of applicants are able to meet the legislative requirements-
So, in addition to an applicant's own family physician examining him, the department wants a specialist to make an examination. That really burns me up, Mr. Chairman.
-whereas, had the specialists' reports not been obtained, many would not meet the criteria-
In other words, many applicants are more or less forced to go at their own expense to see a specialist. Is that fair to the ordinary citizen, or even to the doctor who originally examines the applicant?
-many would not meet the criteria to be determined to be disabled under the legislation; that is, if the decision had simply been based on the report of the family physician only.
I suggest that is partisanship at work there. Many applicants would be rejected if the family doctor only examined them. Therefore, through you, Mr. Chairman, I would ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to clean up this mess and to put a stop to the unhappiness and unfairness created across Canada in respect of those who do not always have the opportunity to be examined by an internist. I know the minister will reply that every-

one has this right, but how many people have the ability to exercise that right, especially those who are sick and down and out? Some people with cardio-vascular failure can hardly get about. Yet in some cases they are told they can take another job. I suggest the department is being unfair to people who are sick, to those who do not have the fortitude and courage to pursue their application, unless someone does it for them.
There is one other point I should like to make and it relates to women who work and contribute to the Canada Pension Plan on the same basis as men. When a working woman dies, her husband and minor children get not one penny in survivors' benefits, aside from a small death benefit which goes into her estate, unless, of course, they can prove they were financially dependent upon her. Yet widows and minor children automatically collect survivors' benefits when a man dies, the assumption being that wives are dependent on their husbands.
I suggest that the minister take another look at this question. There are today 2,831,000 women in the labour force, which I suggest is ridiculous since more than half of them are married. This is, therefore, no longer a valid assumption, and it is time to end this discrimination in the Canada Pension Plan in both of the situations that I have outlined, including that of the single woman.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to add to the remarks my colleague from Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) made a moment ago. I am referring to a matter which I feel should receive more serious consideration from the minister than at present.
Examination of the items of the supplementary estimates reveal that operating expenses account for about one third of contributions.
Mr. Chairman, we have there a typical illustration of the fact that bureaucracy and technocracy sometimes cost as much as contributions themselves. And that is one of the reasons why our party stressed the necessity of the universality, for instance, of old age security, family allowances and minimum guaranteed income. That would eliminate ipso facto expensive investigations, bureaucratic waste and would further ensure greater justice towards the population since the granting of benefits on an overall basis would preclude omissions and ensure justice.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I believe that a step forward was achieved yesterday. Old age security and the guaranteed income supplement will henceforth total $325 a month, approaching the minimum vital income required by people of 65 and over. However, apparently some considerations have been overlooked, which should have concerned not only the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) but also the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), namely the plight of people aged from 60 to 65, which is very unfortunate.
At 60, Mr. Chairman, people have been working for more than 40 years. Most of those who are now 60 started working at 15, or earlier. And when one has worked for 45 years, one has directly contributed to the progress of one's country; one has also directly contributed, through taxes, its share of the revenue needed for the administration of the country. And when one has reached the age of 60, one
February 20, 1973

is not asking for favours or gifts, one is just claiming his due.
How is it that this possibility has not been seriously considered yet? It is quite surprising. And what happens to people aged 60? They have to call, at least in Quebec-I know the figures-on the Department of Social Affairs which, through its various local offices, grants, not pensions, not a vital minimum income, but rather an indecent pittance for 1973, since they evaluate the needs of a person, for clothing, food and other personal needs, at $39 a month, that is $78 for a couple. Add to this the rent, electricity and some insurance, for theft or fire-if you take the case of a 60-year-old couple that has no income or cannot find any work-and it is impossible for a person to contemplate the possibility to get any income at all. This is why one has to call on welfare services and then, they generally grant a couple about $125 or $130 per month.
If the needs, at 65, are estimated at $324.30, Mr. Chairman, how is it that, at 64, these same needs are estimated at only $125? Why this difference of $200? This is not a question of wondering whether it will cost too much to lower the age of entitlement to 60; we must simply wonder whether it should be done. If so, the cost does not matter because we are facing a deplorable and disastrous situation.
That is the reason, Mr. Chairman, which must prompt us and the minister to consider the matter seriously. And then, we have two alternatives: either the eligibility age is reduced to 60-which would settle the problem of many heads of family-or, as demanded by the Quebec Minister of Social Affairs, the province is entrusted with the care of managing or co-ordinating the entire welfare program.
If the Minister of National Health and Welfare would agree to consider seriously the problem so as to reach a realistic conclusion in that field, we would solve some very serious and painful problems for the Quebec government.
Mr. Chairman, it would be more than ever advisable for the government during this session to assume its responsibilities and to consider immediately the possibility of introducing a bill to reduce the eligibility age for old age security pension from 65 to 60.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to add to the length of this debate and I agree with everything that has been said, but I was particularly interested in the fact that the minister did not reply to the hon. member for Oxford and the hon. member for Simcoe North.

He might indicate how we, as members, can assist people in isolated areas who do not have access to heart specialists or internists. Some of these people are only now having their requests rejected, and I ask the minister to give us a reply in a written form for the edification of hon. members.

Mr. Chairman, since the main estimates have been tabled and will be before the various standing committees shortly, if we get this kind of information in detail from the minister at this time it will prolong our consideration. I should like to add a few words to what my colleagues have said concerning people aged 60 to 65.
This is sad, but these people are very penalized in their life and it is impossible for them to find a job now. When they lose their job, they are discriminated against because of their age and their performance.
Reference has been made to various solutions; it has been suggested that we lower pensionable age to 60. My party has made many proposals in this respect. Apparently, the government turns a deaf ear to our representations. Nowadays, you always hear about freezing this and freezing that. Perhaps I would make a suggestion which would be a lot less expensive, in view of the fact that the government is short of money: we should freeze people when they reach 60 and wake them up when they get to 65. This way, we could save a fair amount of money.

Mr. Chairman, I have a very brief remark to make. I think the minister implied a moment ago that he was ready to take notice of our suggestion and comment on them at the end, that is, in his own speech.
I have always noted-and this is confirmed by last night's budget-that older people are considered differently depending on whether they are heads of families or not. The head is granted the sum of $170 in addition to the guaranteed income supplement, whereas-

Order. I think the hon. member for Lotbiniere was in the House yesterday when the Chairman of Committees of the Whole (Mr. McCleave) referred to Standing Order 58 (13). I doubt he can be recognized a second time as he spoke before. Besides even the minister did not have the opportunity of replying.

[The Deputy Chairman.]

Mr. Chairman, I would not like to interfere but if some points need to be clarified, it is up to hon. members to ask me questions.

I am ready to co-operate with the party officials to accelerate this study mainly because the budget debate will take place soon, because a bill amending the Old Age Security Act will be introduced and finally because the estimates will be referred to the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee.

That could be one of the first orders tackled by the committee.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; I think the decision is not up to the acting something of the Conservative party but rather is up to the minister. Because of the detailed questions which were asked by the two members, I had asked if we could be given a written critique. An article was recently published in a daily newspaper of the Ottawa-Hull area on bilingualism in the House of Commons, particularly among the protective staff. I imagine-

of Commons has nothing to do with government administration and cannot be discussed at this time in committee.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to the item for inter-parliamentary relations which we are asked to vote, I recall a trip to Washington within the framework of Canada-U.S. inter-parliamentary relations. I then met representatives of the American government. It was at the time we were discussing salaries, working conditions of hon. members, senators and Congressmen. My hon. colleague from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) is aware of that. His party was very ably represented by his colleague from Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin).
Mr. Chairman, I recall the discussions that took place then and which greatly interested our American colleagues. The state of the Canadian Parliament was being considered. Our American friends, within the framework of inter-parliamentary relations, came to Canada and I had the honour to be among the delegates who received them. I recall that at a supper in the National Arts Centre, the discussion bore precisely on this typical aspect of bilingualism in the House of Commons.
The Americans were very surprised of this situation and they were enthusiastic and they congratulated us.
Mr. Chairman, so that countries with which we have interparliamentary relations get a better image of the House of Commons, I suggest that the minister who requests the adoption of vote 5a should ensure that in inter-parliamentary relations we not only discuss better friendly relationships between countries but we should also emphasize this particular feature of Canada as a country that we want to recognize as bilingual and bicultural.
Consequently, when representatives of foreign countries are welcomed to the House of Commons, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me the members of the security staff should get equal treatment, with regard to competence and salary, when it comes to the official languages. Mr. Chairman, why not give an interesting picture to the representatives of those countries, within our inter-parliamentary relations-

Mr. Chairman, I anticipate staying in order because we have support for the estimates, the bill, and if necessary for the budget. The only thing that bothers me is the influence of the hon. member for Yukon, but really

that has not been much. It has been more of an irritant than a deterrent.
I am interested in two problems connected with the vote dealing with accommodation. I notice that we are erecting a number of single purpose and general purpose buildings, and I am interested in one general purpose building that simply is not being built. It has appeared in and disappeared from estimates with some regularity. But before dealing with it, since the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Public Works are both present I would like to deal with what I consider a fairly serious situation in terms of parliament, with respect to the vote just passed.

speechtext: Order, please. I certainly do not want to reflect on the Speaker of the House. I know he does not have such poor taste as to put a green rug in a blue room. It was not his fault. Obviously, it must have been done by the Department of Public Works. All I want to know, either from the President of the Treasury Board or from the Minister of Public Works, is what happened to the rugs, and why can't we have them back? It is my guess somebody took them home.
Prove it.

I want them brought back.
What I am mainly interested in with respect to this supplementary estimate is why provision is not made for a new federal building in my riding at the Earlton airport. The Prime Minister came into that area last summer, and gave an indication to the people there that he was surprised that the airport was operating with pre-war facilities.
Which war?

In Northern Ontario we flew off water most of the time during the first World War, so the facilities must be pre-Second World War. Good airport facilities have been built at Val d'Or and Rouyn. I ask the minister to give serious consideration to replacing the building at Earlton, which is obviously obsolete.
As I have said, this building was previously mentioned in supplementary estimates, but does not appear in this

estimate. It also appeared on several occasions in the main estimates. I believe a terminal should be erected there such as was built at Rouyn. Rouyn has a municipal airport. The Department of Transport owns the airport at Earlton, and a new building could house both radio technicians and weather technicians, as well as other facilities operated by the federal government. I make the plea that the minister discuss this with the Prime Minister who at least has had the opportunity to be there. I believe this is a reasonable request as I have already waited for 15 years. I think the people of that area should have a similar service to that being provided on other routes. It seems very odd to fly from a nice airport in Montreal to Ottawa, Val d'Or, Rouyn and then come to the archaic facility at Earlton, and on to the good facilities at North Bay, all on the same route.
I hope that the minister will give consideration to this minor expenditure which would provide a facility which is badly needed already, and will be more so in the future since that airport is now servicing three airlines and a very large flying club.

Mr. Chairman, this is too good an opportunity to miss. On several occasions since I became a member of this House, I have asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube) to look into the matter of retaining walls along the St. Lawrence river. Either I did not get answers or they were in the negative, that is they did not mean a thing. I am surprised about this because we often get more co-operation from other departments. Finally, I did get excellent co-operation from this department through its Victoriaville office.
The St. Lawrence contains unheard of wealth. It is the largest inland waterway of the world and it flows along the constituency of Lotbiniere as well as others on both shores. I am sure my Quebec colleagues recognize the importance of this situation.
Quite some time ago, the federal government would agree to build retaining walls, piers and harbours, but despite the legitimate representations made by municipalities, by the people of these areas and hon. members -regardless of party-nothing has been done in recent years.
Mr. Chairman, the primary consequence is an obvious danger of erosion along the St. Lawrence, specially on the south shore in the Lotbiniere area. Along the St. Lawrence the land is constantly eaten away by tides and the passing of ocean liners, in the narrowest straits of the river, notwithstanding the content of the department's studies.
And through you, Mr. Chairman, I would tell the minister on the occasion of the budget debate that it would be extremely important for himself as for Canadians that he commit himself to review his department policy to earmark a portion of the credits granted by the House to protect a natural resource such as the St. Lawrence River.
I do not quite understand why at a time the federal government invested several thousand dollars to build wharves and retaining walls whereas today it allows to be
February 20, 1973

destroyed what was built and is not even prepared to study the dossiers.

Mr. Chairman, my colleague mentioned the south shore of the St. Lawrence River and as my constituency is located on the north shore, we have similar problems.
I have been trying for five years to have the minister understand that the standards which have been adopted when the retaining walls were built are inadequate and nothing is more astonishing not to say insulting for the St. Lawrence riverside dwellers than to be told: The standards are not met. The shipping channel is over 3,000 feet away and we cannot undertake this responsibility.
They completely disregard the concrete fact that there are dwelling along the river. Behind those dwellings, there used to be 100-foot backyards but one day the owners woke up and saw the river under the veranda! Considerable damages are made to properties by landslides. More time should be devoted to study this problem.
In some places and among others at Sainte-Marthe du Cap-de-la-Madeleine and at Champlain, Highway 2, which is only a few feet from the river, will eventually be damaged. Why wait then for disastrous damage to happen before changing standards which, in my opinion, are inadequate. They are the more so since statistics show that, until 1967, all retaining walls built along the river were entirely paid for by the federal government. Since 1967, it has been decided that the standards would be changed. I do not know what happened in the course of one year that the situation was so radically changed.
There have been expensive investigations made during the last two years. I think a few million dollars were spent for an investigation into this matter and retaining walls would have cost about the same amount. Then, let us put an end to investigations.
Whether the minister likes it or not, damages are being caused by navigation. We must now take into account that navigation is going on all year round, even in winter. Therefore the movement of ice resulting from the maintenance of the river, even in winter, is increasingly eroding riparian land. In my opinion, navigation is always indirectly responsible for most of the damages.
In fact, Mr. Chairman, how could one explain for instance the complete uprooting of trees which had grown for over a hundred years on the shores? If those trees could grow for 100 years, it means that nothing stopped them from growing. So why are they gone today? It is because of year-round navigation, and I think that problem is one the minister should attempt to solve since spring is already here and it is the best time to assess the damage. The minister should therefore send people down to size up the situation, review the standards of his department and do justice to those who live along the St. Lawrence River and are unable to remedy that situation themselves.
And when they are told that 75 per cent of the damages could be paid when they total $200,000, for example, even a contribution of 25 per cent is prohibitive for the riverain owners in the municipalities of my riding, and none of
Supply
them would be in a position to pay $50,000 to have their property reinforced.
The minister should realize that immediate steps are necessary in order to change those standards.

Mr. Chairman, may I be permitted to say a few words in reply to the recommendations, representations and suggestions made by the three hon. members who have just spoken.
In the case of the representations made by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) with regard to rooms 601 and 602 of the central building, as you pointed out yourself, Mr. Chairman, I think that this question comes under the jurisdiction of the administration of the House of Commons rather than the Department of Public Works. Nevertheless, in compliance with the wish of the hon. member, I will try to find out who ever thought of putting a green carpet in a blue room, or a blue carpet in a green room, and I can assure him that as far as the old Indian carpet is concerned, it is not the Minister of Public Works who brought it home because his wife would not allow it.
As for the second representation, I understand it is about a terminal or some other building for an airport in his constituency; I must say that the airport problem does not fall under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works but under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport. However I am sure that my colleague the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) will, while reading Hansard as he does every day, take notice of the very interesting representations made by the hon. member for Timiskaming and will see to it that he gets justice, especially if it is an airport which has already been visited by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
As for the hon. members for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) and Champlain (Mr. Matte), they dealt with erosion and retaining walls along the shores of the St. Lawrence river. The position of the government in this regard is quite clear: when erosion results from navigation and marine works, we assume full responsibility and build retaining walls; when it results from natural erosion, that is, ice, floods, the causes are natural: the responsibility is not ours but that of the province or the individual, whether it concerns his property, his home or his cottage.
Still, if those two hon. members know of specific cases which really fall within the responsibility of my department, I shall be eager to have retaining walls built where they are needed.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could make a few remarks under the rubric of this aspect of the estimates. They were used extensively by pleasure boaters, being offered as a free service to the boating fraternity. On certain locations of the Severn River, particularly in the west end, mooring points have been closed for the past several years and many boaters have had to use privately operated marinas in the area. I do not see the minister present. Perhaps his parliamentary secretary is here. The question I wish to ask very simply is whether it is the policy of the ministry of transport to close down these public mooring points.

I bring up this matter under the rubric of the Department of Transport estimates because, until recently, the Chambly Canal, part 6f the canal works connected with the Richelieu River, was under the direction of the ministry of transport. I am not sure if there has been any change during the past couple of years in the department which has responsibility for the canal. I say that because the canal has stopped being, in any real sense of the word, a commercial canal and is now almost totally devoted to pleasure needs. The point I want to make is this: during the past few years flooding of the Richelieu River in the region above St. Johns, Quebec, has become serious and it is quite likely that this coming spring the flooding will be worse than that which occurred last spring.
We are told by the experts that the level of Lake Champlain in the United States, a lake which as many hon. members know flows out through the Richelieu River, is 19 inches above normal for this time of year. There was
February 20, 1973

flooding last year and there will certainly be flooding this year. This matter relates to this or a related ministry, because over the last couple of years there have been some very serious changes to the shape of the Richelieu River at St. Johns, Quebec. St. Johns is the point where the river has the first rapid. This is the point where the river and lake levels are effectively controlled. In the past couple of years, there has been a widening of the canal at St. Johns and a consequent narrowing of the river. Therefore, even normal flows of water from Lake Champlain would be restricted. This year they are expecting higher than normal flows of water.
It is important to note that, along with the widening of the canal which has brought about a considerable change in the size of it and the consequent narrowing of the river, there has been no dredging of the Richelieu River below St. Johns in the rapids section since 1942. Dredging should be carried out quite regularly in order to keep the river level below the point where it would cause problems in the spring. I feel that all of these factors combine to increase the natural level of the lake and river waters, but the widening of the canal and the subsequent narrowing of the river as well as the failure to dredge the river will combine to cause very, very serious flooding this spring. Possibly the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Public Works, if he has any jurisdiction over the projects going on there, could comment on whatever steps might be taken to obviate this flooding danger.

speechtext:
that Bill C-12, to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1965 (Yukon and Northwest Territories Senate representation) be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it might be said that my motivation for placing the bill on the order paper arises from the fact that I have spent some 16 years in this place and I am, perhaps, getting a little tired of it and looking forward to a greener and more casual pasture. But really this is not the motivation for the bill. All Canadians represented by members here, save a few, are represented in the Parliament of Canada. Two exceptions to this full representation are the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. It may come as no surprise to some of the older members of this House that this is the case. I am sure quite a number of the newer members here will be quite surprised to hear that this area of Canada, over 40 per cent of the area of the country, and all of those citizens who live north of the 60th parallel, have no representative in parliament as a whole. They have a member in this place. The seat for the Northwest Territories was established in 1949 by a change to the act and, of course, the seat for the Yukon has existed since 1903. From then, I may add, until 1949 one member represented the whole of that vast 1,600,000 square miles.
I want to bring to the attention of hon. members that the joint Senate and Commons committee on the constitution, when it completed its work, recommended that there should be Senate representation for each of these two northern territories. I would hope this alone would cause members to agree to send the bill to committee for, after all, that is all that is being asked on second reading, that the bill be sent to the committee for consideration. Undoubtedly, the committee would go into the recommendations of the joint Senate-Commons committee which held hearings throughout the Yukon and Northwest Territories and, after very careful consideration, came up with the recommendation that indeed these two northern territories should have Senate representation in order to

be fully represented in parliament, not merely in this chamber.
The bill does nothing to affect any Senate representation in any other province in Canada. It retains that Senate representation intact. All it does is add two members to the Senate, making a total of 104, and gives to the Yukon a senator and to the Northwest Territories a senator.
I could go on at great length about government reform and all its aspects in the Yukon and Northwest Territories; reform that is so urgent and spoken of by the minister during the last campaign in real terms of promises of things that would happen when we came back. I shall not do that but will maintain my usual non-partisan approach to matters such as this in the hope that we can get the same kind of co-operation from members opposite that we have shown them over the last several days in getting their estimates and supply bill through. All we ask on this side is that the bill be given second reading and sent to the committee where all its aspects can be examined.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I should like now to address a few remarks to the fundamental question of Senate reform. At the outset, I think it is fair to say that many Canadians lack faith in the Senate as an institution. I am certain that many members of the NDP would like to see the Senate abolished. Personally, I have a very high regard for our distinguished senators, but this high regard does not necessarily carry over to the institution itself. I do not favour abolition of the Senate, but I would like to see it reformed and made more functional. The role of the Senate must be made more effective and more in tune with the needs of the democratic process in Canada.
In recent years, the Senate has taken the initiatives toward making its role in parliament more effective. Hon. members in the other place are to be commended for this action. They have undertaken a number of impressive studies into particular areas of policy, and resulting Senate reports have been both highly competent and thorough. A fair amount of legislative action has also resulted. I should like to mention a few examples including Senator

Croll's report on poverty in Canada, Senator Lamon-tagne's report on science policy, and Senator Davey's report on the media in Canada.
In addition, senators have joined with members of parliament on special joint committees to study such questions as divorce reform and the constitution of Canada. It was my privilege to serve on the constitution committee. I look forward to increased initiatives of this kind emanating from the Senate. I feel the Senate must involve itself more and more in detailed investigation of important questions facing the Canadian nation.
My colleague, the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) made a very concise speech calling for reform of the Senate in the recent debate on Bill C-10 which, it it had passed, would have effectively abolished the Senate. I wish to lend my support to the reforms my colleague suggested, and I would also call to the attention of hon. members the recommendations in the final report of the constitution committee in regard to the Senate. I am hopeful that the Senate, with the full and active support of our eminent contingent of senators from British Columbia, will continue its welcome moves toward greater activity and greater reform.
I must reiterate my very strong feelings that none of these reforms can succeed until the Senate is truly representative of the regions of Canada. The constitution committee made a series of recommendations to achieve this most important goal. The committee recommended that the number of Senate seats be increased to 130, 28 more than there are in the present Senate. The committee recommended that central and eastern Canada maintain their representation at the present level, while western representation should be increased to 12 members from each of the four western provinces. The Yukon Territory and Northwest Territories should have two Senate seats each under the plan the committee felt would best correct the inequities of Senate representation. I do not think that an increase in Senate seats of that magnitude is warranted to solve the distribution problem.
During the course of the deliberations of that committee, my colleague, the former member for New Westminster, and I concurred in a proposal for redistribution of the Senate. I would like to put this proposal forward today for the consideration of all hon. members.
The first thing about the current situation in the Senate, which really drove home to us the inequitable distribution of seats today, is the fact that Ontario and Quebec have 24 Senators each, almost half the entire representation in the Senate. In an institution which is supposed to reflect the diversity of our great nation, this seems to be a most peculiar and unwarranted situation in terms of present day conditions.
It has been a major complaint, and in many instances a fully justifiable one, from western Canada that the interests of central Canada are protected over and above those of the rest of Canada. I do not fully subscribe to this view but I do feel that the inequitable distribution of the Senate adds symbolic fire to the flames of what has come to be known as western alienation.

I propose today that consideration be given to reducing the number of Senators from Ontario and Quebec to 20 from the present 24 as an important first step toward redistribution of the Senate. Then, there is the gross imbalance caused by the over-representation of the Atlantic provinces in the Senate. I have very great reservations about the province of Prince Edward Island having four seats in the Senate when its total population is somewhat similar to my own riding of Kamloops-Cariboo. British Columbia, with a population more than 20 times as great as that of Prince Edward Island, has only two Senators more than the island province. But despite my reservations, I suppose full marks must be given to the Fathers of Confederation from Prince Edward Island for having the wisdom and the foresight to have this entrenched in the British North America Act as part of their conditions for union with Canada in 1873. For obvious reasons, I propose that the present level of representation of Atlantic Canada in the Senate be maintained for each of the four provinces of the region.
I should now like to discuss the crux of the problem of distribution of Senate Representation. In order to redress the inequities of western Senate representation, I suggest that each of the four western provinces have their representation increased to 10 Senators and that, in line with the spirit of Bill C-12, one seat each be provided for the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories.
These proposals would bring the total number of Senate seats to 112, 10 more than at present. It would correct the unjust proportion that the current situation perpetuates. And, with a smaller Senate than that recommended by the Constitution Committee, the same purpose is served as that which was sought by the committee in its recommendations to cure the problem of Senate distribution. Western Canada and the north are the keys to the future of this nation. I commend to all hon. members the need to recognize that reality. Let us make the Senate truly representative of the great regions which make up Canada. When we consider the role of the Senate, let us look to the future, not to the failings and inadequacies of the past.

Mr. Speaker, at this time I should like to make a few comments on the bill introduced by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). I wish to commend the hon. member for expressing his concern regarding more representation for the north. In particular, I am concerned about more members for the Northwest Territories. In making my point, I wish to refer to some of the difficulties members of the north experience in representing that very large part of Canada. I might mention that it is most important, not only for the north but for all of Canada, that the north have more representation because at this time we have only a partially elected and partially appointed legislature for the Northwest Territories. In its present stage, I consider it to be somewhat like a colonial type of government. Within the next few months and the next few years some very important decisions will be made which will affect the native people of the Northwest Territories.
Decisions regarding natural resources and so on in the north are most important to all of Canada. I think wise decisions can be made only if there is sufficient representation from the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory. Some of the problems members from the north face are centred around transportation and communication. It is very difficult for the members from that area to cover that part of the world adequately. For example, a member going from Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories to, say, Frobisher Bay would have to travel about 6,000 miles. This would involve a journey of two days and an expense of $650. The cost of flying in a small aircraft is something in the order of one dollar a mile. Telephone service, where available, is something in the order of one dollar a minute. Therefore, the cost of transportation and communication is very high. The area of the Northwest Territories, which involves 1) million square miles, makes it very difficult for one person to represent all that part of the world.
The formula of representation by population does not allow sufficient representation for the Northwest Territories. Although there are only approximately 40,000 people in that part of the country, the diversity of the way of life of the several peoples in that part is shown by the fact that the languages spoken are English, French, Louchoux, Dog Rib, Slovey, Chipewyan and in some areas three or four of the major Eskimo dialects. A large proportion of the population is unable to either read or write. This, again adds to the difficulty in respect of representing that area. The idea that perhaps we should have Senators representing the Northwest Territories is an idea I cannot accept, because I do not believe appointed people are representative.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to support this measure for increased representation in parliament from the Yukon and Northwest Territories. I am sorry that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Marchand) could not see fit to endorse the bill as it stands as a prerequisite to his efforts toward Senate reform.
Because of the responsibility respecting Indian affairs and northern development which I have been given in caucus, I have been particularly concerned with problems of the north, the pros and cons of rushing resources into development and the way developers and conservational-ists are striving to work together in this area rather than as protagonists. They realize that conservation and development must go hand in hand in the north. There are few

February 20, 1973

places in southern Canada where such an approach has been tried, let alone carried out.
I have met with northern native leaders and believe, as their struggles for equality become more intense, that it is only just that there should be more people in parliament who know their feelings, who represent those huge areas, who are familiar with the problems, who come from that part of Canada which too many people consider to be the periphery and, therefore, too far away to be concerned about.
I have been fortunate enough to have travelled in both the Yukon and Northwest Territories, those remote but very beautiful parts of Canada. It is indeed difficult to appreciate the magnitude of our north. It has always been of interest to me to know that if we were to travel as far south as we can travel north, we would be well into South America. We can appreciate this if we ever have the opportunity to visit Frobisher, Resolute, Cambridge Bay, Inuvik, Yellowknife, Whitehorse or a score of other northern places.
While in the north I felt what most northerners learn to live with, a sense of remoteness and isolation. But for all its remoteness, many of the problems of the north are remarkably similar to those of southern Canada. For too long our northern territories have been considered quaint areas of hinterland into which no one goes because of the cold. It is difficult for those of us who have not spent much time there toappreciate the feelings of long-time northerners, the feelings of the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) and of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen).
The hon. member for Yukon first introduced this measure in 1959 shortly after he was elected to this House. Three years later, in 1962, the hon. member's bill was debated in this chamber. His reasons for urging greater representation for this area which he delineated 13 years ago stand even more firm today and are more urgent because, surely, all Canadians living above the sixtieth parallel have the right to be heard in both Houses of Parliament. While over the years there have been motions by hon. members advocating reform and even abolition of the other place, there has been little or no action. Northerners, all this while, have not had the same sort of representation as other Canadians.
When Newfoundland entered confederation in 1949, the British North America Act was amended to allow for Senate representation of that province. The Northwest Territories and the Yukon have not been accorded the same consideration. I believe that wider representation in parliament by northerners would help those of us from the south whose knowledge of the north is limited, and in many cases is minimal; it would help us to a greater understanding of this vast, rich area that we are privileged to have as part of Canada.
Late last year an organization called Federation of Natives North of Sixty brought together seven Indian, Metis and Inuit groups of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. They felt they needed a stronger voice, particu-lary with respect to land claims. Their particular, yet special problems as natives are compounded by living in the north. I think it would be particularly fitting if a representative of the native peoples could sit in the other
Senate Representation
place for one or both of the territories. I would like to point out that in 1971 the census figures showed that in the Northwest Territories there were 34,800 people, 6,400 Indians, 11,000 Inuit and 17,400 others, and in the Yukon there were 18,400 people, 16 per cent of whom were natives.
Southerners have learned much over the years from hon. members who have represented the Yukon and Northwest Territories in this chamber. I am firmly of the belief that our education can be enlarged and enhanced even further by giving the territories the representation they merit in parliament as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has done this chamber a service in bringing before it Bill C-12 which would have the effect of instituting Senate representation for the Yukon and Northwest Territories. But I regret that his interest in the debate extended only to his own words; he has not remained to hear other hon. members participate.
The joint parliamentary committee on the constitution dealt fairly extensively with this subject and I would like to draw the attention of the House to its recommendations and reasoning. Recommendation No. 71 in the report of that committee provided that the Yukon and Northwest Territories should each be entitled to representation in the Senate. That had been preceded by recommendation No. 38, dealing with the Senate itself, in which the distribution of seats in the Senate as recommended by the committee was spelled out. The recommendation of the committee was that both the Yukon and the Northwest Territories should have two seats in the Senate. It would not usually be possible for a member on this side of the House to describe the hon. member for Yukon as a piker, but in this case he has not gone so far as the recommendations of the parliamentary committee.
Turning now to the chapter in the report of the committee dealing with the constitution of the territories, I should like to refer to the comparatively brief reasoning given with respect to Senate representation for the territories. The paragraph I shall quote is the last one on page 65 of the report which reads as follows:
In order to improve communications between Ottawa and the territories at the parliamentary level, we advocate immediate Senate representation for each of the two territories. Under the constitutional rule that a province cannot have fewer members in the Commons than in the Senate, the appointment of two Senators for each territory would lead to an increase in the number of Members of Parliament to two for each.
Perhaps this is the reason the hon. member for Yukon, not wanting company in representing his part of the world, has chosen to stay at the figure of one. Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, I should now like to turn to the chapter in the report of the constitution committee dealing with the Senate where this matter is more fully canvassed and put into the perspective which the hon. member for Yukon attempted to prevent this House having. I will first read some of the comments of the committee at page 35 of the report as follows:
Two regions, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, remain without representation in the Senate. There is precedent for
