having senatorial representation for the territories. In 1888 the Northwest Territories were first given two Senators under the authority of a constitutional amendment of 1886. This was increased to four in 1904 prior to the acquisition of provincial status by Saskatchewan and Alberta.
I interject at this point that of course the geographical area of the territories was somewhat different before the creation of the western provinces, so that statement may be somewhat misleading. But so far as the theory is concerned, there is no more reason now why both territories should not have Senate representation than there was in this period earlier in their history. Continuing on the same page of the report of the constitutional committee I read the following statement:
Two of the most obvious deficiencies in the current distribution of seats are: (1) the disparity in representation in geographical and other terms between the western provinces and the other provinces; (2) the fact that the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, being a major part of the Canadian land mass, are not represented at all in the Senate.
As the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Mar-chand) has pointed out to the House, this matter cannot be considered in isolation from other changes which should be made in respect of Senate representation. For instance, I would not allow my preference for two seats for the territories, as opposed to one which the hon. member for Yukon is recommending, to stand in the way of referring this bill to committee, but I think we should recognize that in the public mind, at least in many parts of Canada, there is just as much urgency with respect to increasing representation from the west generally and not just providing representation for the territories. If this matter is to be seriously considered by this parliament and referred to a further stage for discussion and debate, it might be well to include such a provision.
The constitution committee, of which I had the privilege and honour of being joint chairman, conducted hearings across Canada. It found consistently that when people spoke about the Senate they did not want abolition, they wanted reform. They wanted a Senate which would function somewhat differently but, above all, they wanted a Senate which they felt to be more representative of the people of Canada. It seems to me that this fact is also relevant to the consideration which members of this House are giving, not collectively but individually, to the question of redistribution which is presently under the aegis of a commission.
From my discussions with many members it seems they hold the view that this House should not be based entirely on the principle of representation by population but should somehow include regional representation. I would agree with the bare minimum limitation of the "Senate rule" which protects the province of Prince Edward Island. I trust my hon. friend from Kamloops-Cariboo was not serious in suggesting that Prince Edward Island should have fewer than four Senators or four members of this House. There has to be some minimum for this very important part of Canada, the smallest province.
Surely the principle of representation in this House has to be that of representation by population, just as the principle of representation in the Senate surely has to be one of geographic or regional representation. I believe

this is the principal reason for having a Senate-not for sober second thought in legislation, although this is one of the advantages. The fact of regional representation is the raison d'etre for the continuation of the Senate in the Canadian political system.
This is the theme which the constitution committee heard again and again across the country and everywhere in the west. The plea was made that the west had to be more adequately represented in the Senate, that its representation should be doubled or that all provinces should have equal representation in the Senate. The committee very seriously considered this question of equal representation for the provinces-something like ten Senators for each province. I suppose this would be, by way of analogy with the American system, a feasible way of arranging representation in our Houses of Parliament. We decided to stay closer to the present distribution.
As the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo indicated, there was some division among members of that committee with respect to the number of seats that should be allocated to the various areas, but I think everyone agreed that the number of seats for the west should be dramatically increased.

Mr. Chairman, on a number of occasions concern has been expressed regarding the deadlines which we are trying to meet in the passage of these supplementary estimates.
In the past four days.

I have been advised that with respect to the Manpower and Immigration programs, allowances to persons on Canada Manpower training courses, LIP grants and further payments in respect of LIP grants under the 1972-73 program and contract payments to companies giving on-the-job training to unemployed workers, all further payments in respect of these programs will have to be suspended commencing February 22. On that date the funds available for these programs will be exhausted. Without further parliamentary authorization it will not be possible to continue to make payments.
Similarly, on the same day, Thursday, with regard to 74,700 recipients of war veterans allowances who are normally paid on the third last banking day of the month, unless approval is received by February 22 for mailing them, they will be delayed by the number of days beyond February 22 that it takes to secure royal assent to this bill. I might add that in addition to the 74,700 recipients of war veterans allowance there will also be similarly affected 3,300 recipients of civilian war allowances.
I appreciate the necessity and desirability of giving adequate consideration to the estimates but we wish, if we possibly can, to meet these deadlines.

Mr. Chairman, on the point that has been raised by the minister, we have been very keenly aware of the consequences of delaying these estimates. We were aware of this in committee. We sat long hours there, as we have here. We were Thursday, Friday, all day yesterday and today trying to get all the items passed without debate, and all stages of the bill. I want to again put on record that in the debate while we have been in committee of the whole 32 New Democratic Party members and 18 Social Credit members have spoken. With 46-member representation in the House, they have had a total of 69 speakers. When these are added to the Liberal speakers, we have had a total of 85 speakers. We in this party have had 33 speakers.
Hear, hear!

So that there will be no mistake about our intentions of seeing these estimates through, we are pre-

Mr. Chairman, I shall begin by asking the Minister of State for Urban Affairs a couple of relatively simple questions of a non-controversial nature. When I have asked these questions and received the quality of answers that I expect to receive, I should like to make some general remarks about the item in the schedule.
During a question period a few weeks ago I directed a question to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs with regard to tri-level conferences, federal, provincial and municipal. I understand the minister has been encouraging these over the past year, particularly during the past few months, and that there have been conferences between governments. However, there is considerable evidence that there is interest in particular localities to hold tri-level conferences of elected officials. For example, a conference of elected representatives in a community or small town could involve federal members, provincial members, municipal councillors, members of school boards and, possibly, leaders of community associations. It would be an extremely good way of having the elected members from a locality get together to understand the problems of a locality and, better still, to work out a concerted program for themselves, working, as it were, in harness.
I know the minister said several weeks ago that the federal government was more than ready to encourage and assist tri-level conferences. I do not want to distort his answer to the point of saying he would similarly encourage tri-level conferences of the more informal kind I have described, but would the minister not take this possibility under consideration? I repeat that it is an excellent way in which elected representatives can get together to work out problems and also to set projects for themselves.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. In light of what has been said with regard to procedure, I shall make all my points in one fell swoop, as it were. But they concern very different subjects and I thought they could be dealt with more easily if I kept popping up and down.
I wish to ask another question of the minister. It has to do with a statement he made this morning on the subject of rent freezes in projects directly controlled or managed by CMHC. I am thinking particularly of limited dividend projects. I know of projects in Toronto which use standard forms of lease as the contract between the owner and the tenant. These forms contain a clause which provides, in effect, that the rent agreed to shall remain fixed unless approval of an increase is given by CMHC.
I invite the minister to look into what has happened regarding 230 Oak Street. Tenants of this project signed leases on December 31, only to be advised two days later that their rents would be raised, the owner having received permission to do so from CMHC. In the private business world such a thing would rarely occur. The minister should take into consideration the circumstances in which it is possible to raise rents in these circumstances. He should consider making the rent freeze retroactive at least to the beginning of this year, because a number of rental agreements were signed by tenants around December 31.
The estimate has to do with research in housing and community planning. More money is to be devoted to such research from allocations which apparently have already been agreed in the House. There are one or two areas which ought to be examined very seriously. Everyone who has studied housing is aware that one of the most serious problems facing those who enter the housing market is that of raising money, in some cases, and the high interest charges applied to those who borrow it.
Many of us remember years when an interest rate of 6 per cent was considered high for a prime mortgage. For a number of years now the standard rate has been between 9 and 10 per cent. There is no doubt that such rates, seen in historical perspective, are usurious. Interest rates on domestic mortgages are prohibitive. It is not long ago that the minister, in order to help more people buy houses, raised the limit which could be borrowed from CMHC to $30,000. I wonder how many members have calculated the

Supply
amount of interest which has to be paid on such a sum over the life of a mortgage. The total amounts to $42,000.1 wonder how many people have calculated the length of time the average man has to work to pay off this $42,000, not counting the principal and leaving aside the down payment.
In Toronto, where I live, the average industrial wage is about $4 an hour. That figure is probably high, but let us take it to be $4 an hour. At $4 an hour a person can expect a gross income of about $8,000 a year. We all know the Canadian Tax Foundation tells us that a person earning $8,000 a year with the usual number of dependants-in this case let us say two-will pay about 37 per cent of his income in taxes of all kinds. If you subtract this 37 per cent in taxes from $8,000 a year, you are left with a net income of $5,100. If you divide the $5,100 into $42,000, you will see the number of years that the average working man has to put in just to pay the interest on the property he has purchased for himself and his family.
People have suggested in the past few months that something must be done to bring down interest rates. Perhaps some suggestions have been a little utopian, but I am sure very few hon. members would agree that an interest rate of, say, 61 per cent or 7 per cent is utopia. I am sure several members of the House have bought their homes in the past at this rate or at a higher rate. It was not too long ago that many of us considered a rate of 7 per cent to be high. But let us say that by various devices-I hope to suggest one or two in a moment-we could bring down interest rates by 21 per cent, or in other words reduce them from the 9 to 91 per cent level they are now to a 61 to 7 per cent level.
If I may again entertain the committee with a few more calculations, let me suggest that the saving in the interest payments over the life of a mortgage contract brought about by a reduction in the interest rate of 21 per cent would amount to about $17,000. Again going through a process of rough division, we find out what is the net income of the average wage earner over the course of a year, and we discover that by bringing the interest rate down by 2} per cent we will save him, in effect, some three years of work in that lousy factory or that boring office, work that is devoted solely to earning money to pay off this 21 per cent interest. It is not devoted to the other 7 per cent interest, or to the principal he has had to put into the house as a down payment, or to buy food or shoes for his kids, or to put money aside for entertainment or travel; it is devoted solely to paying off that 21 per cent.
Let us ask ourselves what we are doing with all these grand programs that we use in pretending we are helping the working people of this country, when we cannot come to the stark realization that the better part of a working person's life is devoted to paying off the interest on the mortgage he takes on his house. No one can tell me that a lot of people do not buy houses. I know that a lot of people rent them, but if you rent rather than pay off mortgage interest on your own house you are merely helping to pay off the mortgage on the landlord's house, which is really the same thing.

Suggestions have been made with regard to ameliorating this situation. It has been suggested, for example, that people with a certain income should have their mortgage interest subsidized. That is a fairly good suggestion but I think it would be too indirect and would apply to too small a percentage of the population for it to have any real effect. As hon. members know, many other suggestions have been made to reduce the original cost of housing. However, in the past we have had many figures proving that by far the most massive part of the cost of housing is the cost of money and the cost of land.
Some time last year the minister suggested establishing some kind of mortgage clearing house-I forget the exact title-in which the lending and financial institutions of this country would be encouraged to invest more money for lending purposes; I think they were his very words. I have a few suggestions to make in that regard, suggestions that could be forwarded to the research groups that will be doing further research into housing and community planning. Although it does not always appear to us to be the case, there is a fair amount of money in this country available for investment. I am not suggesting that the government has its hands on very much of this money. When one looks at the figures showing the amount the government has available for discretionary investment- that is to say, amounts that it can or cannot, may or may not, place into certain areas-the amount is relatively small when one considers the vast sums that are now under the control of the financial intermediaries of this country. By "financial intermediaries" I mean banks, lending institutions, trust companies, insurance companies, and so on.
I will take just one example from among these financial intermediaries and deal specifically with trustee pension funds. Those of you who have been looking at the figures over the past few years will have noticed that trustee pension funds have grown in size; not alarmingly, but certainly rather strongly, to say the least. In 1960 the total assets of the trustee pension funds amounted to $3.5 billion. In 1970 they had grown to some $11 billion, and of course it goes without saying they have grown since then. That is not hay; that is a lot of money.
What is done with this money? According to a publication by Statistics Canada, this money is spread over various forms of investments such as bonds, government bonds at all levels, municipal bonds, school bonds, and so on. The Minister of Finance is not here, but let me point out to the President of the Treasury Board that the proportion of these funds invested in government bonds has gone down considerably over the past few years. A fair amount of money is invested in stocks, and the proportion of money invested in stocks has gone up rather strikingly over the past ten years.
In other words, trustee pension funds, in carrying out their design to make money, are finding it more lucrative to invest their money in stocks. It is also rather alarming to discover that there has been a very marked increase in the amount of money invested in stocks of non-Canadian companies. I can try to flummox this committee by saying that the increase over the past ten years has been 71 times, though perhaps that would be a little misleading since I am merely following a trend.

The figure I want to concentrate on in relation to assets of trustee pension funds is the amount devoted to mortgages. We find that in 1960 the proportion that was devoted to mortgages of all kinds-not necessarily residential mortgages or mortgages on family dwellings or single family homes, but mortgages of all kinds-accounted for 8.3 per cent, and this amount has grown enormously over the years and now accounts for some 9.2 per cent of the total of assets invested by trustee pension funds.
What I am getting at is this. If we were to do a little more in this country than simply saying to these companies that they must invest in safe securities, and we said to them that not only must they maintain the security of the original investment placed in their hands in trust but they must also invest a certain proportion of their assets in socially useful projects that would satisfy the real needs of Canadians, then we might find that this would have a significant effect on the interest rates of domestic mortgages in this country and indeed on the whole field of housing.
In other jurisdictions, particularly the one to the south of us, there are financial institutions, savings and loan companies, for example, which are forced by law to invest a certain proportion, be it 30 per cent, 40 per cent or 50 per cent of their total assets in domestic mortgages. That is why in the United States mortgages are more easily available at lower rates than here in Canada.
I would suggest to the Minister of State, through you, Mr. Chairman, that rather than even invite these financial institutions through a form of encouragement to invest in what is, after all, a vital necessity, one of the elements which ought to be produced in quantity by our economy is investment by these people in the area of domestic mortgages. Rather than even encouraging them to invest, they should be told to invest. One does not have to be radical or drastic about it, telling them they have to invest 40 per cent; this could be progressive and conservative-
Oh, oh!

I suggest that pension funds in trust could be used for investment in domestic mortgages to the extent of some 5 per cent a year for the next four or five years. I will not go into specific calculations because the point is obvious. If this large segment of our economy, financial institutions which do nothing more than hold the savings of the nation in trust for us, was told to put our savings to use in the realm of mortgages, particularly the domestic mortgage market, we would find that in a relatively short time not only would there be more mortgage money available but the cost of that money would go down.
This government in the past has effected a two-price program for various commodities. Why should we not have a two-price program for mortgage money, a certain price for the commercial market and another price for the domestic market, being the average individual who wants little more from us than the possibility of buying a home for his wife and children? I hope to come back to this point on a number of other occasions, perhaps this spring
Supply
and again next year. What I suggest at this stage is that this is an area in need of considerable attention.
A few weeks ago I asked the Minister of Transport a question regarding the CNR pension fund with particular reference to a horrible example. A number of years ago when I was a boy at school I was a rather clumsy person. One of the seniors said to me, "Don't worry, Harney; no one is totally useless: you can always serve as a horrible example." The CNR pension fund is not totally useless; it serves for us as a horrible example. This pension fund is held in trust for the workers of this country who are, in effect, direct employees of this government. This is a pension fund over which the workers have almost no influence-I will not use the word "control"-yet we find the fund invested in mortgages and other fields. This money is invested in what kinds of mortgage?
Let us consider the Fidinam case. The fund loaned $33 million to this foreign corporation to build another fancy office building in Toronto, and I assure you we did not need another fancy office building there. One thing we need in Toronto, Montreal and other communities in Canada is mortgage money at reasonable interest rates for these workers whose funds are being held in trust. Without going very far, not even to the private lending institutions, we could take some of this money held in trust for the public and parapublic workers of this country and put it to work building houses, rather than fancy office buildings wholly controlled by foreign corporations. Some of these office buildings were built with money raised totally in Canada and, in too many unfortunate cases, from money raised from those employed in our public institutions.
I have another suggestion in respect of a program quite dear to the heart of the previous minister in charge of housing and CMHC. I refer to the special and innovative $200 million program for low-cost housing. There was an interim report which came out in May of 1971. I believe originally $200 million was put into this program, with $100 million added to it. I would very much like to see a full report on that program in order that we may determine how the money was used. There are many questions in many areas of the country that need to be asked about this program, perhaps in no area more particularly than the province of Quebec.

If I may, Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with the $200 million program and ask whether we could perhaps get an extensive report explaining in detail how this money has been invested and how it has profited Canadians.
One need not enquire very long to realize that people, particularly in Quebec, are very dissatisfied with this program.
Many construction projects have proven to be failures. Tenants and landlords are unhappy and dissatisfied with the quality of housing that was built for them. I could give a list of the projets-this would only take a moment-that should be closely inspected to see-

Mr. Chairman, I think I should say a few words about Bill C-141 and mainly about item 10a, which is of particular interest to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford). This item appears on page 53 in Supplementary Estimates (A) and reads as follows:
To extend the purposes of Urban Affairs Vote 10, Appropriation Act No. 3, 1972 to reimburse Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for expenditures incurred during the period January 1, 1973 to March 31, 1973 on housing research and community planning.
Mr. Chairman, clearly, like any responsible corporation, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation employs research personnel, people who conduct analyses. In the present case, the analyses are naturally specifically related to residential housing in our country.
In view of complaints reaching us from Ville Belair, Val Saint-Michel and even Ville Vanier and other locations in my constituency, I am led to wonder, Mr. Chairman, at what level the studies have been conducted, and to what end? Were these studies fruitful? Did they focus on improving the quality of houses or on downgrading it?
Mr. Chairman, I am wondering about those things because, as the previous speaker stated, there has long been discontent in Quebec. I have here an article in the October 27, 1971 issue of Action Quebec, titled as follows: Owners of Place Pierre-Bertrand are under the impression that they have been had.
Those owners are angry. They all feel they have been cheated on their houses, costing an average of $14,000. The building defects found reveal that residential standards of the building code were absolutely disregarded.
On the occasion of that meeting, the members of that association stated, and I quote:
The federal government is involved in this matter because the Place Pierre-Bertrand project was subsidized by the housing department.
Furthermore, according to the majority of owners present, there may have been collusion between the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the contractor in order to avoid an inquiry, since they say that had there been an inquiry, the houses would never have been accepted.
So, Mr. Chairman, such is the situation for a particular area. I have here another letter from Neufchatel. It is addressed to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, it deals with file No 430-LH-19861 and is signed by Roland Simoneau, Neufchatel. Mr. Simoneau writes:
This is to inform the CMHC about flaws and defects in my house.
Clause 7 of my contract provides that:
The borrower shall, during the period of this loan, keep in good repair the said building with dependencies and make all necessary repairs, and representatives of the lender and the Corporation . .. can inspect it on occasion ...
So he wonders:
How can I keep in good repair a house I received in bad condition?
He goes on:
Is it any wonder that it costs us $300 to heat three walls when the seller told us it would cost $130, which is quite a difference.
[The Assistant Deputy Chairman.]
Moreover, since the inspector from CMHC never came to inspect the house, has he the right to come five years later when the inspection has never been done . ..
You understand that it is impossible to look forward to the future in such a house. The builder does not honour the guarantee he gives us, he probably wants to wait until the five years have passed. How can we fulfil our commitments? We might just as well move into rented housing again; this experience has been enough.
Mr. Chairman, these are the impressions of an owner.
After examining a house in Neufchatel, Mr. Louis Carrier, a Quebec City architect, said this:
This report was prepared following an on site inspection on Wednesday, September 27, 1972-
It is three pages' long. It is the inspection of a small $14,000 house, and I quote further:
(1)	FOUNDATION:
The main front foundation wall is inclined outwardly by 11" at the top-
(2)	FRAMEWORK:
(a)	In the basement, the center beam is made of four assembled 2"x8" beams. In violation of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation's standards, cuts in the composing parts are located 6" beyond the bearing center (or the steel column).
Moreover, this beam should rest on a pilar when meeting the anti-fire dividing wall instead of being imbedded in it.
(b)	In the basement, a wood column, made of two 2" x 4" frames for the girders along the staircase and bearing a goundfloor partition, is truly defective-
(c)	The groundfloor floor framework does not meet the standards of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The 1 5/8" x 7 1/4" beams, spaced 164" center to center, stand out 12'- 21" which is inadequate since the C.M.H.C. minimum requirement for this wood (Eastern spruce) holding living quarters is: 2" x 8" beams . .. with 16" spacing center to center-
Because of this inadequacy, the floor sank by at least 1 " at the center of bearings, namely in the middle of the living room, kitchen and bathroom.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the Minister of State for Urban Affairs a question which is important to cities the size of Yorkton which I have the honour to represent. It concerns relocation of rail lines in downtown centres. Can he tell the House when we may expect some financial assistance for the relocation of rail lines from the downtown cores of cities of this size, and what will be the amount of such financial assistance? One point I wish to stress is that I would not like to see this assistance go only to the CNR and the CPR. I am concerned that when the program comes into effect too much emphasis will be placed on larger centres such as Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. Cities the size of Yorkton are very interested in this matter. Perhaps the minister can comment later this evening on this point.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the minister three short questions for which I am sure he will have answers. What steps has he taken to implement the Liberal election promise to build an $80 million waterfront park in the city of Toronto? Either the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources made such a promise just prior to October 30 last, hoping to gain political capital. The good citizens of Toronto realized that this was the aim.
As a supplementary question, Mr. Chairman, I ask what citizen participation will be involved in this park. It will be a big job to co-ordinate the efforts of the federal, provincial and municipal authorities in assembling the land, designing the buildings and carrying through with the program. I hope local citizens will be involved in this work.
My second question is: when will the minister bring forth the CMHC capital budget? Further, does he anticipate including in that budget the programs he has set forth in Bill C-133, the bill he recently introduced? If they are not included in the CMHC budget, how will he fund the rehabilitation program, the NIP program and the other programs mentioned in the bill? I heard the hon. member from Hamilton asking about the NIP program: it is the Neighbourhood Improvement Program.
My third question concerns the guarantees the minister promised with regard to defective materials and workmanship in the construction of homes. The previous speaker for the Creditiste party mentioned some of the disasters that have occurred in building programs. The provisions in the new bill presented by the minister only go to a certain extent and include the completion of work by a builder who becomes bankrupt. Many people have had work done with CMHC and NHA financing which was later found to include defective materials and bad workmanship. Will the minister be introducing separate legislation with respect to building guarantees, or will they only be included as part of the new bill he has introduced?

I have one or two questions to ask the Minister of State for Urban Affairs on the question of urban renewal, which concerns all municipalities. Two or three weeks ago the minister indicated that there are changing trends in urban renewal. If I remember correctly, he said that we were going to place more money in and

greater emphasis on the re-establishment and rejuvenation of already established neighbourhood communities. I commend the minister for this new trend. In other words, we are not going to concentrate so much on the bulldozer, but on rebuilding and rejuvenating existing communities. Going back as far as 1968 and 1969, many municipalities across this country have drawn up position papers and gone to a great deal of expense in order to establish urban renewal in the context in which we interpreted it ten years ago-in other words, the brick and mortar, blast and bulldozer approach-to clear out downtown urban areas and rebuild.
I represent the riding of Brant. At the present time the city of Brantford has budgeted approximately $2.3 million for a downtown urban renewal program which takes in the former market square which was established as a result of the construction of the city hall 112 years ago. Some of the merchants in that area are struggling, and this development would put capital and retail trade in their direction. Brantford city council has budgeted $2.3 million for market square development.
I ask the minister whether funds are available to a municipality for this kind of development under what might be called the new terms of reference of his department with regard to urban renewal. I listened to the minister but, Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that the taxpayers' money should go toward commercial development. I wonder whether there are still funds available for this kind of development, even though eventually this downtown market square development in the city of Brantford will be entirely privately owned and commercially oriented. Could the minister reply to this question as well?

Mr. Chairman, I am going to be very brief. I only wish to direct a question to the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation (Mr. Basford).
Could the minister tell whether his department could ensure that CMHC stops lending money to contractors who build bad houses, unhealthy houses, and who come back year after year, under a new name, to build shacks in other towns with the approval of CMHC? I wish the minister could tell us whether his department intends to find mechanisms to control this situation.
At present, the building industry is growing ever faster. A 24' X 40' house with a 1140-foot floor area, built of "Gyproc" and heated by a forced-air system, costs about $18,000, whereas last year the same house was selling for $16,100. The individual who buys such a house must meet payments during 39 and often 49 years under the new system; often the house is built to last no more than 10 or 15 or 20 years. What I am about to suggest could protect the money invested by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as well as protect the consumer.
We are rather lucky around Sherbrooke. I know of no contractor who builds such shacks but I did visit some in Montreal, for example, where the situation is terrible. Last year, we saw 34 houses that could not be sold by the contractor and yet the inspector from Central Mortgage and Housing had been there and had approved those
February 20,1973

houses. The builder could not sell them because you could see right through the walls, Mr. Chairman. It was as gusty inside as outside. I went there in the month of July. This was called the "Nid d'abeilles (Honeycomb)" project or something of the sort. I do not remember exactly but in any case there was a sleek word in the name. The sewage system had not yet been put in and I think that the city around Montreal where those houses were located thought it would be desirable not to instal the system too rapidly because the houses were not selling.
If a man who knows nothing about construction refuses to buy a house which was built by a contractor and checked by two or three inspectors from Central Mortgage and Housing who are supposed to know their business, how is it that those things can go undetected by those who seek to protect the consumer and would like him to be happy in his one-family or multi-unit dwelling.
In view of the high demand for housing again this year, I would ask the minister if it would not be possible to have Central Mortgage and Housing to thoroughly research the matter so as not to let the consumer be fleeced in such an unreasonable way.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:

Many of the questions can be dealt with at great length and exhaustively when the main estimates are considered in committee. There we can review the issues that have been raised. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may seem anti-climactic to shift in midstream from the important matter of money consideration to the more mundane matter of human lives. Your Honour will recall that at the close of the debate on capital punishment on January 31,1 was cut off, with good cause, in mid-sentence at the very peak of oratorical excellence. As I recall, I had sympathized with the protagonists of capital punishment who because of their emotional bondage to the topic felt bound to call for the blood of all those convicted of homicide, but I had rejected emotion as suitable grounds for a decision.
I have since noted that most of the speakers who rose in self-righteous indignation to demand the blood of convicted killers have at the same time demanded with equal vigour an end to the slaughter of innocent civilians in Viet Nam, both North and South. I had rejected the arguments based on statistics as well on the grounds that in effect liars figure and figures lie. I sometimes think that if all statisticians were laid end to end, it would be a good thing.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL

There is no proof that capital punishment is a deterrent to capital crimes, as other speakers have pointed out. I will not dwell on that aspect of the topic. Revenge, too, it seems to me is too base a motive for settling such an important issue and can be dismissed out of hand.
My suggestion was that any favour in which retention was being held was possibly due more to the frustration of society with seeming permissiveness-a section of the public is ready to lash out at all those who violate the laws directed against homicide, despite the futility of capital punishment as a deterrent, despite the ambivalence of arguments based on religion and despite exhaustive studies by qualified authorities.
I had reached the point, then, of examining the question from a philosophic point of view. What is it, I asked, that separates man from the rest of the animals? Not reason, because some animals have shown the ability to reason in various degrees. The one thing we can do that animals cannot do is to store experience. While the animal, generation after generation, teaches its young in the same way, through example and experience, mankind is able to store his experience through history books, literature, artifacts, monuments and the like. Despite this superiority, however, I pointed out that there still lurks the beast just below the sophisticated veneer of modern man. The reason I gave for this was the relatively short period of time during which man has been on this planet, taking into account the tremendous span of life forms. Man has

February 20,1973
Capital Punishment
been on earth a relatively short time in comparison with the entire scale of life-the continuum of life in all its forms on this earth.
At the close of the session I was about to paraphrase an example used by a Dr. Mdller. I ask you to imagine a rope stretching from Toronto and ending at the Speaker's chair in the House of Commons. This rope will represent the entire scale of life from the very beginning of life forms to this date in 1973. Now, scientists have estimated that life forms have existed on the earth for something like a thousand million years. On a rough scale, therefore, we might say that one yard of this imaginary rope represents 10,000 years. One human generation would be represented by less than one-eighth of an inch. On that scale of life we would find the dinosaurs making their first appearances at the entrance to the Commons chamber.

It is for this reason that we are still able to employ, despite the sophistication of our technology and the growth of our experience, such bestial methods in the wars, terrorist activities and homicidal acts which take place every day all over the world.

Mr. Speaker, I ask that this House get out of the business of killing and into the business of co-operating to find workable alternatives to protect our society. subtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL
subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Today we are talking about abolishing or retaining capital punishment but I must say that I would have liked it better if we had started with a debate on the causes of crime before discussing its punishment.
A lenghty debate on the means to bring about a genuine reform to the whole society, to its judiciary system, its penitentiary system, its rehabilitation system for those on the fringe of society, would have been still more meaningful than the one we are having today.
If genuine and efficient means of rehabilitation and, most of all, crime prevention could be guaranteed and provided to the society, it would mean that we would have to establish throughout the country adequate rehabilitation programs because I would agree with the hon. Cyrille Vaillancourt who said that there is no use in trying to rehabilitate those on the fringe of society if, at the same time, they are taught to do wrong.
We are now worried about the life of the murderer, but not about the causes which led him to commit a crime.
When criminals are jailed, are studies made of their life and their past to find out about the reasons why they got there?
Since there is little certainty that abolishing the death penalty would be beneficial to our society, which is responsible for the protection of the community, and in view of the fact that most citizens of my constituency are in favour of the death penalty, I cannot vote in favour of the bill now under study.
Abolitionists say that there is some danger of condemning innocent people. If it can be proven that judicial errors were committed in the past, it is not the penalty that should be changed, but the judicial proceedings on evidence and doubt.
Even though governments throughout the world seem to be moving towards abolition of the death penalty, they do not do so with the support of the majority of the people. The most recent Gallup poll in Canada, published in February, 1972, showed that almost two thirds of Canadians want the death penalty to be reinstated, after the five-year trial period, in the case of murder.
If it is true that we represent our electors in the House, I think that it is logical to vote on this bill, in accordance with the wishes of most of them. Some members regularly speak in favour of retaining the death penalty and at the same time, some citizens would like other crimes such as kidnapping, rape and drug traffic be also liable to death penalty. Public opinion remains inexorably in favour thereof; most people, especially police officers and prison guards, feel it is effective; therefore, that view deserves to be upheld. It would almost be impossible to find another punishment to be substituted for the death penalty; even long-term imprisonment is not sufficient and the custom of an early parole makes it less effective.
i
February 20, 1973

On the other hand, life imprisonment which, in my opinion, is more cruel than death, leaves no hope to the criminal and does not lead him to repent as does the prospect of an immediate death penalty.
And if one does not think sufficient the reason that public opinion in Canada is definitely in favour of capital punishment and that it should not be abolished against the will of the majority of Canadians, let us consider that the law enforcement authorities are of the opinion that death penalty is an effective deterrent against murder, particularly since it deters professional criminals from procuring weapons and committing acts of violence.
In a country such as Canada, which is young and in full development, where the people are a mixture of several nationalities, there is a greater need for a deterrent such as capital punishment than in some other countries, in Western Europe, for instance, which have been constituted over a longer period of time and in a much more homogenous way in terms of race, language, religion and mentality. The incidence of murder and the proportion of premeditated homicides are higher in the United States and Canada than in western Europe. The abolishment of capital punishment would therefore involve a greater risk in the United States and in Canada than in Western Europe; it would result in a recurrence or an increase of crimes of violence. Furthermore, those who resort to violence are predominantly professional criminals for whom capital punishment is a more effective deterrent than mere detention, to which they are already accustomed and which they tend to consider as a professional hazard.
The Royal Commission of Inquiry stresses the fact that any world history teaches us that the threat of imminent death is the most effective deterrent there is. Death is death and there is no better description of the terror it inspires. When capital punishment really exists, would-be killers has little or no conception of his changes of not ending his life by the executioner's hand. Capital punishment therefore retains its deterrent effect. When homicide is committed, it is evident that the deterrent effect of capital punishment failed, but that does not mean it did not prevent many others from committing a homicide. When a murder is premeditated, it is not logical to suppose that its author would ordinarily have thought of the danger of getting caught and its consequences.
Most statistics that do not usually show up the death penalty as a deterrent are gathered by abolitionists. In other words, their figures are not compiled with a view to drawing a conclusion; they are gathered instead to confirm a conclusion already arrived at through moral, philosophical or even intuitive reasoning. Statistics lend themselves to various interpretations: they are doubtful and misleading. It is next to impossible to make useful comparisons between countries, because of the differences in legal definitions of crimes, government department and court customs, political, economic and social conditions.
That is why, instead of suggesting the abolition of the death penalty for the next five years, I would suggest on the contrary that the House agree to vote its reinstatement for the next five years.
That way, we would be in a position to get the comparative statistics we need to discuss coherently either a per-
Capital Punishment
manent abolition or permanent reinstatement of the death penalty.
We would then have available the data required to compare the last five years to the forthcoming five, and such a comparison would indicate clearly whether or not capital punishment has a deterrent effect on criminals.
Of course, I would suggest that alternative only if the House were unwilling to vote in favour of permanent reinstatement of the death penalty.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the debate that has preceded me on the subject of capital punishment, I find it difficult to advance any arguments which have not been previously articulated. Thus portions of my address may sound repetitious and familiar. None the less, as the elected representative for Winnipeg South Centre I feel it is my responsibility to express the feelings of my constituents on this very important matter.
Like all other hon. members, I have received great quantities of mail with regard to the issue of capital punishment. While letters have been written espousing the abolitionist position, the great majority of my correspondence, 80 per cent in fact, has come from those within my riding who advocate the retention of the death penalty for murder in Canada. I believe their biases are similar to those held by the majority of Canadians. As such, the death penalty for murder should be reinstated. Personally, I favour the retention of capital punishment. However, I would prefer to see some flexibility incorporated in any amendments to the Criminal Code.
The arguments offered by my constituents for retention of capital punishment are similar to those put forth by most Canadians. People make reference to the Bible, to statistics and to the deterrent effect of a death penalty. Even though the Bible is contradictory on the subject and says "thou shalt not kill," many quote what they see as a biblical axiom, an "eye for an eye". The Bible says that society has the right to put a murderer to death. Numerous people in my riding believe that the current government, which is society in this case, is fulfilling neither its moral obligation to its people nor its Christian obligation to God.
The crime rate is rising in Canada, and while statistics prove little or nothing most people believe that abolition of capital punishment would, among other things, only aid and abet organized crime in its current expansion into Canada. People are afraid. They are afraid of being mugged, robbed and beaten. We as politicians have all witnessed this fear. During an election people are afraid to open their doors to us and our fellow campaigners. They peek out from behind closed doors, bolted with chains.

They would not even open the door then. Policemen are afraid. So are prison guards. What protection do they have, or have they had during the past five

February 20, 1973
Capital Punishment
years when the government has granted clemency in every capital case? The hired syndicate gangsters and others who commit premeditated murders have had little to fear since 1967 and would be even less afraid with abolition. The death penalty prevents a criminal from repeating his offence. Hanging may not deter murderers, but it sure gets rid of them.
Several years ago in Winnipeg a man named Westgate murdered a young secretary in a local hotel. Sentenced to life imprisonment at the Stony Mountain penitentiary, Westgate was a model prisoner. He earned a free pass or leave to go to Winnipeg, whereupon he proceeded to murder another girl in the same hotel. He repeated his offence. I could cite numerous other instances where murderers have repeated their crime, but this is unnecessary. The point is clear. Most people believe that it is time the government gave some thought to the innocent victims and their families.
Abolitionists point to studies showing that a halt in executions leads to no increase in capital crimes, that the death penalty has not been proven to have a deterrent effect. Such studies include all murders, a great percentage of which result from disputes between persons who know each other, and this percentage probably cannot be deterred by penalties of any kind. However, a great many people are sure that hold-up murders and similar crimes can be reduced in number by the fear of death, particularly if that death is imposed quickly rather than after years of legal delays. To determine whether a murder was premeditated or impulsive is impossible. That is why people believe there must be a uniform penalty applicable to all murderers.
While I am in favour of the capital penalty, I disapprove of the rigid inflexibility of a uniform penalty for all murderers. Every person is different. So is every murder. This is to be considered in any future legislation. There must be clearly defined maximum and minimum penalties for murder, dependent upon the nature of the crime. Obviously, a premeditated murder by a hired killer deserves more severe punishment than the impulsive murder committed by a drunk in a fit of wild anger. Judges must be empowered to levy sentences which fit the particular crime. It is only through legislation incorporating such flexibility that any law on capital punishment can be said to be just.
In conclusion, my constituents definitely favour capital punishment for murder. I feel likewise, but would like to see a greater degree of pjj^ncy injected into any legislation. It is not capital punishment that is barbaric, but murder. Capital punishment seeks retribution, and not vengeance as some have implied. This retribution is what my constituents demand. I feel that their desire is characteristic of the majority of Canadians. Because of this fact I think it is necessary for parliament to retain the death penalty for murder in Canada.

While the abolitionists . .. may argue over the morality or even the effectiveness of the death penalty, neither side seems to have questioned the validity of a number of polls that have been conducted and show quite clearly that the majority of Canadians are in favour of capital punishment.
-majority of Canadians are convinced that dangling a man from the end of a short rope is a deterrent to crime or justice well-served or an effective protection for society-
... it is the responsibility of those who are opposed to capital punishment to persuade and convince enough other Canadians to their way of thinking to form a majority.
But is it the right of our members of parliament to enforce what is now a minority opinion down the majority's collective necks?
-when the vote comes in Ottawa let it reflect the will of the majority of Canadians.
That poses the question: what is the will of the majority? Like other members of this House, I have received a large number of letters expressing all points of view and I wonder whether the several hundred letters I have received are really representative of the majority opinion of my constituents. Some of the opinions expressed are as follows:
We are shocked at the increase in crime and feel that the authorities must help the police, who badly need the death penalty restored.
Another opinion is:
I wish to urge you to vote in favour of the bill being presented to the House on capital punishment. This legislation was a positive step forward in our system of justice-a step toward civilization. Please do not let us slip back to legal murder.

This is another opinion:
Why should we not punish criminals with a Canadian "Siberia" in the north, building settlements, railways, airports, pipelines?

Those who favour capital punishment do not do so for the fun of it, or for the sake of justice; they all believe that the government is much too soft and indifferent towards law-abiding citizens.
A lawyer who is a friend of mine had this to say to me:
Among the criteria for sentencing, the example factor should be considered-if punishment is not severe enough, there is the risk of a relapse.
It is difficult to determine which punishment would be best suited in each individual case.
In our permissive society, however, this penalty seems the most adequate punishment.
It would be advisable to suggest to the capital punishment abolitionists that they should oppose wars.
Surely the murderer does not share the opinion of those who want the death penalty to be maintained.
We often hear: it is better to let a criminal go free than to hang an innocent.
February 20, 1973

However, before a convicted person is condemned, there are four stages to go through before the final decision is made.
1)	Trial before jury: 12 citizen jurors.
2)	Trial before the Court of Queen's Bench: 5 judges.
3)	Trial before the Supreme Court: 9 judges.
4)	Mercy request to Cabinet: 30 ministers.
It should therefore be realized that 56 persons have to have their say before the accused is condemned to death.
Perhaps sentences could be commuted if we knew for sure that the convicts would not be paroled too soon.
I think that the Parole Board legislation is adequate but they are not properly enforced. Paroled convicts are not properly supervised by our probation officers.
It has never been, and it will never be proven that a criminal was deterred from committing murder by the death penalty.
This was a lawyer's opinion.

On a number of occasions during this debate hon. members have quoted from the Bible. Let me refer to another opinion as follows:
When Noah stepped out of the ark God changed some of the rules of society. First he added animal meat to man's permissible diet but forbad the eating of blood. Then he instituted capital punishment:
"And surely your blood of your lives will I require; at the hand of every beast will I require it, and at the hand of man; at the hand of every man's brother will I require the life of man. Who so sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made He man. Genesis 9:5-6.
Thus the institution of capital punishment was based on the doctrine of creation. And the sanctity of human life was to be protected by making murder a capital offence.
Later we find this statement:
Capital punishment is a command, not an option. Gentile governments have the responsibility to maintain the sanctity of human life. God's command for doing this is: "At the hand of every man's brother will I require the life of man."
Then we find this statement:
Mercy is often in order. But to terminate the use of capital punishment, and to remove it from the law books of the land, whether by courts or by cabinet... or by parliament, is national disobedience to the word of God. And the nation, like the individual, shall reap what it sows.

subtopic: FINANCE-MEETING OF FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL FINANCE MINISTERS-DISCUSSION OF MEANS TO RELIEVE TAX BURDEN ON RURAL RESIDENTS

speechtext:
Hon. ]. A. MacLean (Malpeque): Mr. Speaker, on January 15, as recorded at page 269 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) the following question:
Adjournment Debate
Will the minister be seeking jointly with the provincial ministers of finance means of relieving the tax burden on rural people? I ask this in light of the fact that the number of people employed in agriculture dropped by 31,000 in the recent 12-month period.
It was reasonable for me not to expect a definitive reply on the subject matter of the discussions which I hope the Minister of Finance held with his provincial counterparts until the budget was brought down. Now that the budget has been brought down, I expect I will be told that the problem is solved and I have nothing to be concerned about. Undoubtedly I shall be told this, for two reasons. It will be said that the problem is looked after, first because the government has seen fit to remove, under certain stringent conditions, the capital gains tax on a family farm when a farmer dies and the farm is passed on to a member of his own family. In that connection, I feel the imposition of this tax in the first place was an unwise move. I think its partial removal does not go far enough. I believe a capital gains tax should not apply to a farm when passed from father to son during the life of the father. I do not think a farmer should have to die in order to obtain the benefit from this supposed tax relief.
Second, no doubt I shall be told that the inclusion of municipal taxes imposed for local school purposes in the equalization system will have some resulting benefit to the poorer provinces. This is true, and I welcome this item in the budget. However, I am not satisfied that these two measures alone meet the problem on which I based my question. The second budget proposal I mentioned does not give any relative benefit to a rural or urban area. In his budget speech, the minister spoke of the hard pressed property owners. Perhaps this is the case. Because farmers in the business of agriculture must own a great deal of real estate and, due to the trend over recent decades of larger and larger farms being encouraged under the farm credit system in which all levels of government have indulged in recent years, where large loans have become popular and more liable to be approved than modest loans for modest operations, the trend has been that farms have been getting bigger and bigger. However, it does not follow that their earning capacity has been increasing in proportion to their size.
The farmer finds that his capital investment in land is being taxed more heavily by municipal school boards which base their tax on real estate values chiefly for educational purposes. These taxes must be paid whether or not the farmer is making a profit, and the rate of taxation often bears no relationship to the potential productivity of the land in question from an agricultural point of view.
I recognize this as primarily a provincial responsibility, but there is an urgent need for improvement of the assessment methods used in assessing real estate for tax purposes. Many cases can be cited where farmlands are assessed, and therefore taxed, on values which bear little resemblance to their potential productive possibilities or to their profitability as farms. They are valued because of their potential as land for a subdivision, or in my province quite often because they contain a waterfront with a beach, or something of that sort. This creates a situation where the farmer who has waterfront property is forced to pay a higher rate of tax than one who does not.
I think my time has expired, Mr. Speaker.

February 20, 1973
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. I.-Roland Comtois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-MEETING OF FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL FINANCE MINISTERS-DISCUSSION OF MEANS TO RELIEVE TAX BURDEN ON RURAL RESIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, replying to the question of the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean), I would like to remind him that the budget which the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) introduced in this House last night includes many provisions that will help alleviate substantially the tax burden of people in rural areas. Some of these provisions are extended to all Canadians, including those in rural areas, whereas others are intended specifically for rural people.
Among the former is the increase in the basic exemption from $1,500 to $1,600 for single persons and from $2,850 to $3,000 for married couples. I should also mention the reduction of 5 per cent in the basic federal income tax and the provision for a minimum reduction of $100. This provision is particularly important in that it will allow for reductions in federal income tax of up to 100 per cent in the case of low income people. It is estimated that these measures will take 750,000 people off federal income tax lists and I think it is reasonable to assume that a great number of them will precisely be people from rural areas.
Among the measures dealing specifically with people in rural areas one has to mention that which provides that from now on family farms, upon decease of the owner, will be transferred from one generation to the other without being subject to capital gains tax.
Mr. Speaker, when referring to the tax burden of people in rural areas, mention is often made of the heavy land taxes that these people have to support; obviously, this is not a federal responsibility-and I think the hon. member for Malpeque will agree-but one must point out the broadening of the equalization formula proposed in the budget which will ensure that local school taxes on properties are included in the equalization formula.
Since those equalization payments will represent roughly $190 million during the next fiscal year, this means that about 28 per cent of local school taxes levied in certain provinces will be compensated by that amount. I hope substantial benefits will accrue to taxpayers.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention that other steps to alleviate the tax burden of people living in rural areas have been proposed; for example, the federal sales tax exemption granted on equipment and machinery purchases for farm production purposes.
In brief, Mr. Speaker, this shows that the federal government looked very seriously into the problem raised by my hon. colleague from Malpeque and proposed measures which will contribute to reduce substantially all those problems.

subtopic: GRAIN-REPORTED ADVICE BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE TO FARMERS ON AMOUNT OF WHEAT THAT SHOULD BE PLANTED
GRAIN-REPORTED ADVICE BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE TO FARMERS ON AMOUNT OF WHEAT THAT SHOULD BE PLANTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 22 I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to clarify a statement which appeared in the press where he was reported to have advised the farmers of western Canada to plant some 30 million acres of
[Mr. MacLean.l
wheat. He subsequently said, and I of course accept his correction, that he was misquoted. At this point, however, I would suggest that the government, in the person of the Minister of Agriculture or the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, should clarify its position in regard to the market outlook and the plantings they are recommending to the grain producers in western Canada.
In a press release dated February 19, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board said that as of March 1 some clear direction in terms of initial prices and recommendations in regard to plantings would be forthcoming. In discussing this matter in the House I said that it would be useful to have these recommendations before the Standing Committee on Agriculture so that they could be properly examined and farmers would know the objectives and be able to study them.
We find now that the United States government has said it is going to bring some 15 million acres into production that would otherwise have been withheld as a stated policy of that government. We know that policies regarding production can change in other countries, which will effect Canadian farmers substantially. It is in these circumstances that I ask the Minister of Agriculture to clarify his position and that of his colleague and to tell us what their aims are.
The minister in charge of the Wheat Board is currently sending out a questionnaire of sorts to farmers in western Canada asking them what type of acreage payments they want, whether they want them to apply to grain, or how they want them to apply and what their intentions are with regard to planting. I do not know whether this questionnaire will clarify or confuse the situation. In a press release of February 17, the minister said that permit holders must weigh heavily the responsibility of possibly causing an overproduction of wheat by deciding upon distribution on a per bushel basis. On one hand he is worrying about an overproduction of wheat, and on the other hand we have had statements indicating that we should be going all out in grain production.
I think farmers might do well to take the advice of Mr. E. K. Turner, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, who is reported in the Globe and Mail of January 31 to have said that farmers in western Canada should sow 22 million to 24 million acres of wheat this year in order to meet market commitments, and that about 14 million acres of barley would be needed. Mr. Turner told a pool meeting in Saskatoon that we would probably need that much barley and about 31 million acres of rapeseed.
If these two ministers would hold a meeting with some of the farm leaders in western Canada, I think they might receive very good advice. In turn, the farmers would be given better direction than is the case now. I therefore ask the Minister of Agriculture if he will clarify the position of the government so that the farmers may know clearly its assessment of the present market potential and what assistance they can expect in terms of initial prices and guarantees of delivery for grain production in the coming year.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: GRAIN-REPORTED ADVICE BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE TO FARMERS ON AMOUNT OF WHEAT THAT SHOULD BE PLANTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying to the hon. member's question may I repeat, as I said originally, that at no time did I say there
February 20, 1973

should be produced 30 million acres of wheat. I think the hon. member accepted what I said. I say that to clarify the situation. The mention of 30 million acres arose from the newspaper man quoting a member of the Saskatchewan wheat pool who expressed the fear that farmers in western Canada might produce 30 million acres of wheat.
When the newsman spoke to me he said that farm leaders in western Canada had intimated that they would produce 30 million acres of wheat this year. I said at that time that I had never suggested this. I had suggested that farmers should produce all kinds of grain; I included farmers producing grains in all parts of Canada, not just those of the west. A tremendous amount of grain is produced in western Canada. We know that it is possible to increase the production of grain with present cultivated acreage. By using weed control and fertilizers we can increase production by at least 25 per cent in one year. I might inform the hon. member that I met with fertilizer suppliers from across Canada, particularly western Canada, earlier this year and they told me that farmers are buying fertilizer and storing it and preparing for exactly what the hon. member suggested.
May I refer to one or two other matters. We talk about the United States government taking acreage out of land banks and putting it into production this year. According to my information, that government is asking farmers not to produce that much more wheat; they want to increase the production of protein in that country. They want greater soybean production and are trying to encourage farmers to produce additional millions of acres of soybean. We know what has happened to Canada because of lack of proteins for animal feeds. These feeds are very expensive. As well, in western Canada we are still asking farmers to stay in livestock production and even to increase it. We are continuing our grassland incentive program, hoping that farmers will participate in it because we know how important it is.
May I inform the hon. member, if he is not aware of this, that I met practically every farm leader in western Canada before the end of December and asked them the very questions that the hon. member is now suggesting I should ask. At that time the farm leaders made suggestions, although not as many as were made after the erroneous report about 30 million acres was circulated. After that we heard many more expressions of opinion. Perhaps that erroneous report was not so bad in its effect because we found out what people were thinking. To conclude, I have a lot of confidence in the farmers of Canada. They know what they want to do. They are not indentured to anybody, and they know as much as anybody about what can be done. They are the producers of these products.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-OPPOSITION OF CANADIAN TEACHERS FEDERATION TO TRANSFER OF RIGHTS TO FILM VIDEOTAPE TO PRIVATE COMPANY
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-OPPOSITION OF CANADIAN TEACHERS FEDERATION TO TRANSFER OF RIGHTS TO FILM VIDEOTAPE TO PRIVATE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to give some background to the question I wish to discuss tonight, may I refer briefly to an extract of a brief presented by the Canadian Teachers Federation to the Prime
Adjournment Debate
Minister (Mr. Trudeau), dated January 5, 1973. Part of the brief reads:
(iii) That adequate arrangements be made for the full and free use in Canadian schools, for educational purposes, of programs developed with support from public funds under federal control.
The brief continues:
In connection with point (iii) we note with deep dismay that the exclusive rights to post-broadcast distribution of CBC materials are in private hands. In effect, the availability of such materials to Canadian schools is subject to the profit interests of a subsidiary of an American company which is itself a major producer of scholastic materials-
Departing from the text, the subsidiary is Visual Education Centre Limited of Toronto which is thought to be a subsidiary of Encyclopedia Britannica, an American company. The brief continues:
-and which is in competition with the CBC and other producers for sales in a limited market.
That is the Canadian market.
We do not believe that it is proper that the program materials produced by CBC, by a considerable expenditure of public moneys, should be placed in the hands of a commercial rival for post-broadcast distribution on a private profit basis.
It makes the distinction between that which has been produced by public funds and the material used over CBC obtained on contract, through agreement with private film makers or imported from abroad. It is not concerned with that particular material.
We recognize that problems of copyright arise in relation to the post-broadcast use of radio and television materials, and we shall address appropriate requests to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
That paragraph is not exactly central to the point I wish to discuss this evening. It is a copyright matter, but it is also part of the problem. This action of the CBC has caused some concern among teachers and school districts. I believe the contracts have run for about two years. I wish to quote briefly from a letter addressed to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). It is from the Campbell River school district in his constituency. The co-ordinator of instructional resources makes the following points:
(1)	We object to the fact that CBC produces programs with our tax dollar, then sells these programs to a private company who resells them to us.
(2)	We object to the fact that even those CBC programs not purchased by Visual Education Centre Ltd. are being restricted by this same company.
(3)	We object to the fact that televised information from our leaders, in all aspects of Canadian life, as being restricted in its use for our students.
What they are saying involves a bit of the copyright question because for educational purposes it is sometimes necessary to delay broadcasts for rebroadcast at a more convenient time. This is a copyright matter. I repeat that I am not dealing with this at the moment; nevertheless a definite problem exists there.
In the couple of minutes remaining I wish to give a bit of information about this particular arrangement with the CBC and Visual Education Centre. It expires in 1974. What does the contract do? It authorizes Visual Education

February 20, 1973
Adjournment Debate
Centre to distribute educational films. This company makes prints and sells them. By its contract it is also given the right to exploit, sell, market or peddle authorized CBC films. In return, the CBC receives a percentage of the gross sales. It may be that the CBC feels schools are concerned about the fact they cannot videotape copies of CBC educational material. That requires action under the Copyright Act. Nevertheless, there is a very limited market here for Canadian production and the schools of our country, supported as they are by public funds in the same way as the CBC, should have the first crack at access to this material without having to make the payment prescribed by the contract which the CBC has concluded with Visual Education Centre.
I have, I believe, less than a minute left and in this time I wish to make certain recommendations. Though the cabinet may not meet, as requested, with the Canadian Teachers Federation to discuss this question, the minister should certainly do so and use his good offices to discourage the CBC from continuing this private distribution contract for the reasons I have mentioned, and for others which will be adduced by the CTF. Second, the CBC material should be distributed through provincial audiovisual services. Such services exist in every province. Thus, it could be carried out simply. Alternatively, we should set up a Crown distributing system. I believe the former secretary of state at one time suggested such a thing. I am anxious, now, to hear what the parliamentary secretary has to read to me from his prepared statement.

Mr. Speaker, the laws or rules allow the hon. member asking a question to have seven minutes but leave only three minutes to answer, so I cannot give a complete answer concerning the point made by my hon. friend.
But if I refer to Hansard I see that my hon. friend for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) asked the minister whether he intended to meet the representatives of the Canadian Teachers Federation.
In this connection, I would like to point out that this association submitted a brief to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on January 12. Through its president, the federation asked for a meeting with officials of all departments mentioned in its brief, namely External Affairs, Secretary of State, Communications, Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Manpower and Immigration, National Health and Welfare, Finance and National Revenue.
It was then understood that the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) would get in touch with Mr. Sparkes, the president of the federation, in order to set a meeting for the discussion of the brief. That meeting is scheduled for the beginning of next month; March 12 has been suggested but it has not been confirmed yet.
As for the brief, I would like to refer my hon. friend to a part of the introduction of the brief where it is mentioned expressly that the federation recognizes that the provincial governments have the authority to legislate on education. This being said, my hon. friend is well aware of the provincial jurisdiction in that area and he will understand that before making statements, the submission made by the federation, which will get special attention, will have to be examined in detail.
I also refer my hon. friend to the brief where it is said that teachers associations must try to maintain a constant dialogue with their government so that they agree, in view of the anticipated social changes. This is an excellent statement, the contents of which we support and my hon. friend and other hon. members may be assured that the members of the federation and its officials will be welcomed in a very friendly way. With them and with my hon. friend's co-operation, we shall try to examine the various proposals and to find a solution in keeping with the circumstances.
